10075-a-narrative-of-the-life-and-advent:
Venture Smith, a native of Africa who lived more than sixty years in the United States, related his own life story, published at New London in 1798. His preface promises a relation of simple facts, nothing added in substance to what he relates himself.

The narrative follows Venture from Africa through enslavement, labor, and the long road to freedom and independence in Connecticut. Some passages were left out for bulk, the preface admits, but the truth of what remains is vouched for. Readers get a foundational American slave narrative, told in its author's own plain voice.
10835-dr-johnson-s-works-life-poems-and-:
Samuel Johnson's Works, in nine volumes, open with this first volume of 1825, holding his life, poems, and tales. The publishers claim no single author in British literature, not even Addison, offers a richer fund of rational entertainment and sound instruction than Johnson. Their edition aims at an accurate text, with notes where readers need help.

The volume introduces the great lexicographer, essayist, and talker, whose Dictionary and Rambler shaped English letters. Readers meet Johnson the poet and storyteller as well as the critic. The book suits anyone starting a serious acquaintance with the most quoted Englishman of his age.
11134-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-07-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for March 1861 opens with German Universities, an essay on professors and the choice facing American students abroad. Gottingen and Heidelberg draw most Americans, with Berlin growing in fame, but Tubingen, Wurzburg, Erlangen, Halle, Bonn, Munich, Leipzig, and Jena may suit many better. A retired Berlin professor, curious about American colleges, asks what Americans mean by college, just as Americans misunderstand continental universities.

Other pieces include a visit to a German artist, whose portraits seem so lifelike that the visitor thinks he enters a room of living people. Published as the Civil War began, the issue shows the Atlantic's cosmopolitan learning, guiding readers to European study while America itself faced division.
11155-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-07-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for April 1861 opens with April Days, an essay praising New England spring against the fashion of praising only June. Most men, the writer says, choose the fairest pearl of the year's necklace, label it June, and cast the rest away, yet no days are more delicious than those of latter April.

Teams plough the interval, grass greens overnight, blackbirds jangle in the oak, and a hawk sails slowly, stateliest of airy things. The issue also carries a story of iron-mill workers, closing with a dying man beneath pearly moonlight, his dumb soul alone with God in judgment. Published as the Civil War began, the number shows the Atlantic pairing nature writing with stark industrial realism.
11253-the-life-of-col-james-gardiner-who:
Philip Doddridge's life of Colonel James Gardiner follows a Scottish soldier from his parentage and early days through Ramillies, military preferment, and a dramatic religious conversion. Gardiner's letters, domestic life, and conduct as an officer fill the middle chapters, while later sections trace his devotion. charity, and return to England before his death at Prestonpans on September 21, 1745.

Doddridge knew Gardiner personally, and that intimacy shapes the book: it reads as memoir and sermon at once. The narrative treats Gardiner's conversion as the hinge of his life, with soldiering before and after it. Readers interested in eighteenth-century evangelical biography will find a classic example here, earnest and detailed.
11525-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-03-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for April 1859 opens with an essay on agrarianism, casting the old contest of the House of Have and the House of Want as older than Herodotus. Spartan oligarchs, Roman patricians, Norman nobles, and Carolina slaveholders all appear as parties to that struggle.

Other pieces in the number turn to Italy, with cobblers at a street corner in Rome, their song, and their love of scandal, set against Figaro as a high ideal. Literature, art, and politics, named on the masthead, give the issue its range, from argument to travel sketch.
11687-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-03-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for March 1859 opens at Bâle, on the Rhine where Switzerland meets Germany and France. The town looks, one traveller says, like a stranger in a new colony, wearing too much old dress to pass as native and too little to pass as stranger.

Holbein and the dance of death give the essay its subject, with Valentinian's fortress Basilia as the town's Roman root. Later in the number, Dante at Campaldino, Ugolino starved in a Pisan tower, and Francesca murdered by her husband supply materials for the Divine Comedy. The issue pairs art history with Dante's life.
11866-the-life-and-most-surprising-adven:
This 1801 edition presents Daniel Defoe's Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, of York, Mariner, a tale first published in 1719. Editorial notes observe that numerous, almost countless, versions followed, and that several are available in Project Gutenberg's library, a sign of the story's long afterlife.

Crusoe's shipwreck, solitude, and slow mastery of an island have made the book a template for adventure stories ever since. This edition preserves an early nineteenth-century text of the original. Readers meet Crusoe as his first readers did: a mariner whose journal of survival, farming, and building became, for later writers, the model of the castaway tale.
12023-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-11-no-:
The April 1863 Atlantic Monthly, volume 11, number 66, opens with Joseph Severn's paper on the vicissitudes of Keats's fame. Severn, who scarcely needs introduction to Atlantic readers, is paired with an extract from Shelley's preface to Adonais, the elegy for Keats, giving the number a double memorial.

Severn writes as Keats's friend and travelling companion, tracing how a poet neglected in life grew famous after death. A later scientific passage shows the magazine's other side: natural history beside literary memoir. It describes polyps and acalephs divided by tubes rather than vertical partitions, for readers who wanted both poetry and science in one monthly.
12097-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-09-no-:
The April 1862 Atlantic Monthly, volume 9, number 54, opens with a Letter to a Young Contributor. It addresses the many Cecil Dreemes of literature who sign manuscripts with masculine names in feminine handwriting. The editor meets many urgent letters with one comprehensive reply, on how to write and how to submit.

Later pages discuss poetry that describes nature. They note how a poet observes objects that express life in growth and motion, though commonly called lifeless. They follow Clough's sympathies into the revolutionary crisis of 1848 and 1849. The number shows the Atlantic as a working magazine: advising beginners, criticizing poetry, and following European revolution, all in the second year of the Civil War.
12372-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-:
This April 1858 number of the Atlantic Monthly, a magazine of literature, art and politics, opens with personal reminiscences of the Hundred Days. That piece revisits Napoleon's return from Elba in 1815, the brief months before Waterloo, through the eyes of someone who lived near those events.

Around it the issue carries the magazine's usual mix: essays, fiction, poetry and comment on public life, written for educated American readers of the late 1850s. Read whole, the number shows the young Atlantic shaping a national conversation, pairing history remembered first-hand with new writing. It is a snapshot of American letters just before the Civil War.
12373-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-:
The March 1858 Atlantic Monthly, volume one, number five, leads with The Catacombs of Rome, quoting Dante on the parts of Rome that were cemetery to the militia that followed Peter. The essay calls Roma Sotterranea the underground Rome of the dead, where In pace marks the places of martyrs.

Other pieces in the number address European politics, with a passage on liveried lackeys, squeezed peoples, and editors muzzled like dogs in August. The magazine, founded months before, already mixes literature, travel, and reform. The issue shows the Atlantic finding its voice: serious, liberal, and international, with Rome ancient faith set against modern despotism.
12593-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-11-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for March 1863, volume eleven, number sixty-five, opens with Christopher North, a biographical essay. Plutarch, about to write Alexander and Caesar, declares his design is lives, not histories, and that glorious exploits do not always reveal virtue or vice most clearly.

Sometimes a small matter, an expression or a jest, tells character better than famous sieges, great armaments or bloody battles. Portrait painters, Plutarch says, are exactest in face lines where character shows. The Atlantic essay follows that method, in wartime America. The number pairs biography with the magazine's usual essays, fiction and politics, for readers in the Civil War's middle year.
12760-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-09-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for March 1862, volume nine, number fifty-three, opens with The Fruits of Free Labor in the Smaller Islands of the British West Indies. Emancipation, the essay argues, seems at first an uncertain and perilous undertaking, requiring a people to replace compulsion with activity, forethought, alertness, ingenuity, self-dependence and self-control.

To make a free man out of a born slave, in the essay's phrase, demands habits timid, childish and dependent people never learned under masters. The Atlantic, in the Civil War's second year, uses West Indian emancipation to argue for American freedom. The number pairs that essay with the magazine's usual fiction, poetry and politics, for readers weighing emancipation at home.
12794-judith-a-play-in-three-acts-founde:
Arnold Bennett's play Judith retells the Apocrypha story of a Jewish widow who saves her besieged town. Bethulia runs short of water while Assyrian soldiers hold the roads, and its leaders waver between surrender and faith. Judith plans to enter the enemy camp herself and strike at its general.

Bennett keeps the action close and tense, with soldiers, guards, and townsfolk arguing over thirst, duty, and deceit. Haggith and the watchmen give the siege a human scale before Judith's bold act. The three-act form suits readers who want the old tale as stage drama rather than as scripture alone.
12861-theory-of-the-earth-with-proofs-an:
James Hutton's Theory of the Earth, volume one of 1795, laid the ground for modern geology. Hutton argues that land forms, decays, and renews itself through natural operations still at work, from the hardening of strata to the raising of new land above the sea. He answers critics like Kirwan and refutes the idea of primitive mountains.

Field notes from Scotland, including granite seen at Peterhead and Aberdeen, back his claim that heat shaped stony substances. The prose is dense and argumentative, but the idea is bold: Earth has no simple beginning in view. The book remains a founding text for readers of science history.
12882-minstrelsy-of-the-scottish-border-:
Walter Scott's Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border, volume two of the 1806 third edition, gathers historical and romantic ballads from southern Scotland. Historical pieces cover Philiphaugh, Pentland Hills, Loudonhill, and Bothwell Bridge, while romantic ballads include Tamlane, The Douglas Tragedy, Lord Randal, Clerk Saunders, and The Dowie Dens of Yarrow. Notes on local tradition enrich the texts.

Scott also records fairy lore, from subterranean caverns where stolen children cried, to elves and witches blamed for such thefts. The volume shows the ballad collector at work before his novels made him famous. It remains a foundation book for lovers of Scottish song.
12980-the-pony-rider-boys-with-the-texas:
The Pony Rider Boys with the Texas Rangers, by Frank Gee Patchin, sends Tad Butler and his friends onto the trail of border bandits in Texas. The boys leave Delaware Creek for the Pecos country under a midsummer sun, weary, dusty, and sleepy, and soon meet Rangers under Captain Billy McKay. Chapters promise a mysterious attack, a bad man's power, and a cave of bandits.

A captured man named Dunk, accused of riding with McKay's band, is loaded like a sack of meal onto a horse by a laughing lieutenant. The book offers boys a clean adventure of horsemanship, pluck, and law on the Texas border.
14179-theory-of-the-earth-with-proofs-an:
James Hutton's Theory of the Earth, volume two of 1795, gathers facts for his bold geology. Part two treats land rising above the sea, the slow dissolving of the earth's surface, and the forming of soil for plants. Chapters pile examples from many countries, arguing that waste and renewal serve nature's economy. A world without decay, Hutton insists, could grow nothing.

French passages widen the evidence. Mountain nooks that catch rain soon bear plants, and even hard rock faces gain moss, lichen, and trees in crevices. Roots split stone, terraces grass over, and valleys fill with villages, fields, and ruined castles. Hutton's prose moves between English argument and French field notes, but the thesis stays clear: the earth remakes itself through time, lifting, wearing, and rebuilding its own surface.
14528-discourse-on-criticism-and-of-poet:
Samuel Cobb's Discourse on Criticism and of Poetry, from his Poems on Several Occasions of 1707, is reprinted here by the Augustan Reprint Society in 1946, with an introduction by Louis I. Bredvold. Cobb wrote in a letter to Richard Carter.

The discourse defends liberty of writing and fair criticism, praising lofty thought and just eloquence in poets who rule and sing at once. Cobb's verse portrait of the ideal poet-king runs through the essay. The reprint gives students a rare Augustan critical text, short but spirited, from the age of Pope and Swift.
1492-the-life-of-columbus-from-his-own-l:
Edward Everett Hale's Life of Columbus draws on the admiral's own letters, journals. Documents of his time to tell the story from early life through the plans for discovery to the great voyage and the third voyage beyond. Hale lets Columbus speak where the record allows, and fills gaps with careful narrative.

Written, like Brooks's book, for the 1892 anniversary, it is fuller and more documentary in manner, with chapters on each stage of the career. Modern readers will read its praise with caution. It remains a readable source-based life, useful for its documents as much as its tale.
15042-a-narrative-of-the-most-remarkable:
James Albert Ukawsaw Gronniosaw, an African prince, tells his own life in a narrative printed at Bath in 1772 for sixpence and sold by a bookseller in King's Mead Square. An epigraph from Isaiah promises to bring the blind by a way they know not, lead them in paths unknown, and make darkness light and crooked things straight.

Dedicated to the Countess of Huntingdon, the narrative follows Gronniosaw from Africa through enslavement, service and conversion to Christianity in England. Particulars exceedingly remarkable in his experience, as the title promises, include suffering, faith and survival. The book is one of the earliest slave narratives in English, short, devout and direct.
15516-the-religions-of-japan-from-the-da:
William Elliot Griffis, formerly of the Imperial University of Tokyo and author of The Mikado's Empire, published this survey with Scribner in 1895. It traces Japanese religion from the dawn of history to the era of Meiji, and it grew from Morse Foundation lectures at Union Theological Seminary. Griffis dedicates it to that seminary's faculty and to three English scholars who founded critical study of Japan.

The first chapter treats primitive faith before books, the science of comparative religion, and the Parliament of Religions. Later parts, by the book's plan, follow Shinto, Buddhism, and Christianity in Japan, asking how they mingled rather than merely clashed. Griffis takes as his motto the words, I came not to destroy, but to fulfil. The survey remains a pioneering English account of Japan's faiths.
15880-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-13-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for April 1864, volume thirteen, number seventy-eight, issued by Ticknor and Fields in Boston. In the Civil War's third year the Atlantic spoke for the educated North, mixing letters with politics. Essays, fiction, and poems filled each number. This issue opens with a blast against fogies.

Fighting Facts for Fogies argues that young people are right to care little for the past, since the past cared nothing for them. The charge that youth scorns history, the writer holds, is just, and youth is right. Other pieces treat war, art, and public life. The issue shows a magazine willing to quarrel with its elders even while the nation fought.
16002-fardorougha-the-miser-the-works-of:
An Irish novel by William Carleton, Fardorougha the Miser, in his collected works. Eight parts carry the tale of a miser whose love of money warps his home. Carleton, a master of Irish peasant life, writes with humour, pathos, and a keen ear for speech. The novel opens on an August night, clear and cloudless, with a mild, almost continental lustre.

A horseman rides fast down a remote branch road, turns up a narrow lane, and knocks impatiently at a neat whitewashed cottage. A broad female face, wrapped in folds of flannel for a nightcap, appears at a small hinged window. From there greed, love, and family fate unfold. The novel stands as a classic Irish tale: a miser, a household, and money's cold grip.
16513-world-s-war-events-v-volume-3-begi:
Francis J. Reynolds and Allen L. Churchill compiled this third volume of World's War Events in 1919, from the departure of the first American destroyers in April 1917 to the peace treaties of 1919. Articles cover a destroyer in action, Smuts in East Africa, Italy at bay, Zeebrugge and Ostend, American submarines, Picardy, and six days on the American firing line.

Statesmen, commanders, historians, and men who fought all lend their voices. The frontispiece shows Petain about to be made marshal, with Joffre, Foch, Haig, and Pershing behind. The volume gives the war's last years as participants told them, vivid and immediate.
17470-on-the-art-of-writing-lectures-del:
Arthur Quiller-Couch delivered these lectures on the art of writing at Cambridge in 1913 and 1914. He was fellow of Jesus College and King Edward the Seventh professor of English literature, and Cambridge University Press published the lectures. The lectures run from an inaugural and the practice of writing, through the difference between verse and prose, to the capital difficulty of verse and an interlude on jargon.

Later lectures cover the capital difficulty of prose, some principles reaffirmed, and the lineage of English literature in two parts. Readers get a celebrated teacher's counsel on writing, plain, witty, and practical. Quiller-Couch's lectures still serve students who want to write clear English.
17472-yorkshire-ditties-first-series-to-:
John Hartley, born 1839 and died 1915, gathered these Yorkshire ditties in a first series, adding the cream of wit and humour from his popular writings. The London and Wakefield firm of W. Nicholson and Sons published the volume. Hartley writes in Yorkshire dialect, the speech of mill towns and weaving sheds.

Pieces include Bite Bigger, To the Swallow, Plenty of Brass, and The Little Stranger. Babby Burds, Wayvin Mewsic, Stop at Hooam, and The Short Timer follow. Lines on finding a butterfly in a weaving shed, Uncle Ben, and The Old Bachelor's Story show Hartley's range. Readers get dialect verse full of local humour and feeling.
17606-throwing-sticks-in-the-national-mu:
Otis T. Mason, curator of ethnology at the National Museum, wrote this study of throwing sticks, printed in Washington in 1890 from the Smithsonian Institution's report for 1883 to 1884, with seventeen plates. Mason notes three throwing-stick areas: Australia, the Upper Amazon, and the far north of North America. He treats the last group, since the museum held only two Australian specimens and none from the Amazon.

Drawing on collections and research by Bessels, Turner, Boas, Hall, and others, Mason compares throwing sticks from widely separated northern regions and sorts them by details of structure. Readers get a compact museum study of a hunting tool, careful about form and place. It suits readers of anthropology and of Arctic material culture.
18467-the-people-s-common-sense-medical-:
R. V. Pierce wrote this medical adviser in plain English. Pierce was physician and surgeon at the Invalids' Hotel and Surgical Institute, and president of the World's Dispensary Medical Association. The fifty-fourth edition was entered in 1895. The book sold in the millions, revised by Pierce with his staff of associate specialists.

Chapters give physiological anatomy in order: bones, muscles, digestive organs, absorption, blood, circulation, and respiration. The book aims to put medicine in reach of the home reader, explaining the body plainly so that families might understand illness, care, and treatment without a doctor's formal training.
18754-ohio-biological-survey-bull-10-vol:
Bruce Fink and Leafy J. Corrington wrote this Ohio Biological Survey bulletin, volume 2 number 6, bulletin 10, published at Columbus in 1921 by Ohio State University. Fink treats the Lecideaceae, a well-marked family of lichens, while Corrington treats the Peltigeraceae. Fink places the Lecideaceae near the Patellariaceae and other lichen families, tracing growth from simple spores and weak exciples to complex forms.

His notes describe crust-like thalli, dense upper hyphae, and apothecia whose parts fuse with age, with figures to aid study. The papers aim to bring lichen terms in line with general fungus science. The bulletin is a technical but clear source for Ohio lichen study.
18760-wee-peter-pug-the-story-of-a-bit-o:
Ernest Aris wrote and pictured this picture book for Saalfield, the story of a bit of mischief and what came of it. Wee Peter Pug, a small pup, cannot resist his Dame's nice red fluffy shoe and marches off to hide it behind the lawn roller.

Proud of his joke, Peter tells a black kitten, then Mrs. Hen and her chicks, Sir Cockerel, Mrs. Duck, and Billy Rabbit, until a whole procession of garden creatures follows him back. They debate better hiding places, the hen's house, the lake, or the hedge, while Dame still hunts her shoe. The book turns a puppy's prank into a cheerful parade of animal friends.
18823-modern-eloquence-vol-ii-after-dinn:
Thomas B. Reed edited this volume with Justin McCarthy, Rossiter Johnson, and Albert Ellery Bergh, published in Chicago in 1903 as volume two of Modern Eloquence. It collects after-dinner speeches whose authors' surnames run from E to O. The series aimed to preserve the spoken wit and public address of its era in book form.

Inside are short speeches given at banquets and public dinners, where speakers mixed thanks, humor, and argument in a few polished minutes. The pieces show how lawyers, writers, and statesmen addressed a live audience, not a reader. Readers get a lively record of Edwardian public speaking, useful for its style, its jokes, and its view of the occasions that mattered then.
18914-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-20-no-:
Ticknor and Fields published this volume of The Atlantic Monthly in Boston in 1867, covering volume twenty of the magazine of literature, science, art, and politics. The July 1867 number, number 117, anchors the volume, with contents that range across fiction, essay, and poetry. T. W. Higginson, Charles Dawson Shanly, and other contributors appear in its pages.

Among the pieces are An Artist's Dream, The Autobiography of a Quack, and The Bowery at Night, alongside travel and social writing. The Atlantic in this period spoke for educated Northern readers just after the Civil War. Readers get a thick slice of American magazine culture, useful for its stories, its opinions, and its picture of the nation's reading taste.
19082-the-destiny-of-the-soul-a-critical:
William Rounseville Alger wrote this critical history of the doctrine of a future life, here in a tenth edition of 1880 with six new chapters. Ezra Abbot of Harvard added a bibliography of nearly five thousand books on the nature, origin, and destiny of the soul, arranged by topic and time. The work is vast in scope.

Alger surveys beliefs from ancient peoples to modern thinkers, weighing arguments for immortality without partisan heat. He admits the theme baffles logic, yet finds it majestic and worthy of full study. Readers get a learned history of afterlife belief, rich in sources and fair in temper.
19492-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-13-no-:
One March issue of the Atlantic Monthly dates from March of eighteen sixty-four, in the midst of the Civil War. Its lead piece, The Queen of California, plays on San Francisco excitement, while other items cover literature, art, and politics for a northern reading public.

One sketch studies a man's face in close, almost scientific detail, a sign of the age's taste for character reading. As a whole the number shows a great magazine balancing war news, culture, and curiosity, and it rewards readers tracing American thought in wartime. One essay turns to garden scenery, praising Whately's elegant discussion of artificial landscape design.
20096-welsh-folk-lore-a-collection-of-th:
Welsh Folk-Lore gathers the folk tales and legends of Wales in one volume. Fairy tales abound in Wales, the book notes at the start. They share much with like tales in other lands, it argues. That likeness points to a common, very old source for them all.

Each tale has a real and an unreal side, the book says. Many forms of one tale show how old and deep its roots run. Readers meet fairies, ghosts, and charms from Welsh oral lore. The book helps keep tales that lived by the fireside, not in print.
20171-gov-bob-taylor-s-tales-the-fiddle-:
Gov. Bob Taylor's Tales gathers stories by Robert Taylor, a famed Tennessee storyteller. Taylor served as governor and won fame for his fiddle and tales. The Fiddle and the Bow and The Paradise of Fools are among them. One tale tells of a great master playing a wondrous violin.

His bow quivered like a bird's wing as he played on. Each quiver held a melody sweeter than human speech, Taylor says. The hearer fell as if into a realm of visions and dreams. Readers get Southern oral tale-telling at its warmest and most musical.
20282-the-working-of-steel-annealing-hea:
The Working of Steel covers annealing, heat treating, and hardening of carbon and alloy steel. Cast iron holds much carbon as graphite, nearly pure carbon itself. That graphite blackens the hands when cast-iron borings are handled at work. Steel turnings, by contrast, do not blacken hands in the same way.

Such fine points guide the smith in heating and dipping steel in water. The book lays out furnaces, colors, tests, and faults in order. Steelworkers and engineers used it as a shop-floor manual daily. Readers get practical metallurgy from the age of rail, ship, and machine.
20472-grace-harlowe-s-plebe-year-at-high:
Grace Harlowe's Plebe Year at High School, published in 1910, opens the Grace Harlowe series. Plebe was slang for a first-year student. Grace enters Oakdale High School and makes the friends who carry the whole series, among them the sunny Nora.

Nora always saw the best in people if there was any best to see. When a classmate dreads her turn to recite, the girls rally round her. The book mixes lessons, games, and scrapes with a steady lesson in loyalty. It set the pattern for dozens of school stories that followed Grace's class.
20763-carpentry-for-boys-in-a-simple-lan:
Making a box opens Carpentry for Boys, a plain guide to first woodwork. Chapters move through beveling, mitering, and first steps in dovetailing. Mortise and tenon joints get their own clear treatment.

Tools, cuts, and joints build up in a set order for young hands. Each task teaches how any wooden structure is put together. Such books once stood in school shops and home sheds across the country. They prize care, true measure, and patience over speed. A boy, or any new learner, could work through these pages and end with real skill in the hands.
20814-the-psychology-of-nations-a-contri:
War, at its simplest, may spring from the herd instinct of early human groups. The Psychology of Nations takes that claim as a starting point. Predatory urges between groups form one plain reading of why wars begin.

From herds, the study moves to crowds, races, and the minds of whole peoples. It seeks laws for how nations feel, think, and act as one. Such crowd studies bloomed in the years around the First World War. This book, a gift to the philosophy of history, shows scholars then straining to grasp mass feeling with new tools.
22075-the-life-of-duty-v-2-a-year-s-plai:
The Life of Duty offers a full year of plain sermons on the Sunday Gospels. Volume II runs from Trinity Sunday to Advent, the second half of the church year. Each sermon takes the Gospel lesson for its Sunday as its text. The preacher's aim, announced in the title, is duty: faith worked out in daily conduct.

Sermons here treat texts like "alive unto God" and "ye shall know them by their fruits." The style is direct, meant for ordinary parish hearers rather than scholars. Sin, service, and self-examination recur week by week. Such Victorian sermon volumes were household reading, and this one shows the plain, practical teaching once heard in English churches.
22375-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly, volume 17, number 104, appeared in June 1866. The magazine was then a leading American literary monthly. This issue catches the country just after the Civil War ended.

One piece describes parlors in a town called Barton. The two parlors open into each other like no others there. Fine French furnishings fill them, plainer than expected. At the visit described, chairs and tables stand covered for work. Blue yarn, woolen cloth, and cotton lie ready for soldiers' needs. Such scenes show a nation sewing its way back to peace. Readers get period fiction and essays in their original magazine form.
22553-memoirs-of-the-court-of-george-iv-:
Memoirs of the Court of George IV, volume one, covers 1820 to 1830. It draws on original family documents for its court scenes. The queen's case dominates much of this first volume's contents.

Divided opinions respected the queen in the House of Lords. Lord Grenville declared his position in that charged debate there. The Bill of Pains and Penalties was finally abandoned by ministers. The king was left dissatisfied with his ministers' handling of it. Grenville conversed with the king as the affair wound down. Public reaction swung as proceedings against her concluded. Readers get high politics and scandal behind palace doors. George IV's unhappy marriage becomes a national drama in documents.
22656-red-cap-tales-stolen-from-the-trea:
Red Cap Tales retells stories from Sir Walter Scott's Waverley novels for younger readers, as its subtitle jokes: stolen from the treasure chest of the Wizard of the North. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Scott's historical romances, too long and dense for many children, are here shortened and brightened.

The sample finds the narrator at Dryburgh Abbey with a beloved companion. They sit quietly on a rustic bench, gazing toward the aisle where Scott himself lies buried. The pilgrimage mood frames the retellings: to shorten Scott is an act of love, not theft. Tales of Jacobites, border riders, and old Scotland fill the chest. Generations of children met Scott first in such dress, and the book shaped how his stories lived on.
22903-the-expedition-to-borneo-of-h-m-s-:
H.M.S. Dido's expedition to Borneo aimed at suppressing piracy, and its narrative rests on remarkable papers. The writer explains how he drew the story from a man whose career had raised him to high station as a British agent in Borneo. That man shrank from writing his own life, so his rough notes were confided to another's pen.

Behind the modesty stands James Brooke, the White Rajah of Sarawak, whose rise the Dido's cruise supported. The pages mix naval action against pirate fleets with the founding of a personal kingdom. Few imperial stories are stranger than this one. Readers get adventure and statecraft together, told close to the events by men who served in them.
22927-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-18-no-:
Boston's Atlantic Monthly opens its July 1866 number with a strange medical confession. The writer's notes on his own case, he says, were declined by every medical journal he offered them to. The facts were not quite new, editors felt, and the mental conclusions he drew from them were not, in themselves, of medical interest.

That rejected case, a famous account of phantom experience after injury, found its home in fiction's clothing instead. Around it, the issue carries the Atlantic's usual mix of essays, poems, and reviews for a recovering nation. The date matters. America in July 1866 was one year past civil war. A single number like this one shows its best magazine thinking aloud.
23468-observations-on-the-causes-symptom:
J. Kent of Stanton, Suffolk, wrote this medical tract on scrofula, or king's evil, scurvy, and cancer, in an eighth edition printed at Bury St. Edmund's in eighteen thirty three. The book opens with a note that all plants, from hyssop on the wall to cedar of Lebanon, have their essential parts, a hint at his theory of disease.

Kent was moved by how common these ills were and how little the public knew of their causes and signs. He sets out his views and adds cases cured by his own peculiar mode of treatment. The prose is earnest and plain, aimed at sufferers and their kin rather than at learned doctors. Modern readers should treat its cures as history, not advice, while valuing the book as a window onto early nineteenth century medicine and its hopes.
23800-contemporary-american-composers-be:
Rupert Hughes published Contemporary American Composers in Boston in 1900, a study of the music of the United States, its present conditions, and its future. With critical estimates and biographies of the principal living composers, it also offers portraits, facsimile musical autographs, and compositions.

Hughes opens with Schumann's welcome to the young Brahms, the master crying, Behold, the new Messiah of music. Hughes confesses he is one of the unregenerate who refuse that rating, but praises Schumann's open heart to new beauty. That spirit, he says, marks the true critic. His book applies the same openness to American composers finding their voice.
24171-the-wedding-day-the-service-the-ma:
John F. Hurst edited this wedding gift book, published in Buffalo in 1889 with copyright in 1888. It opens with a full form for the solemnization of matrimony, in which the minister joins a man and a woman in holy matrimony before God and witnesses. A marriage certificate and a witnesses page follow, ready to be filled in and kept.

Later pages turn from the ceremony to the home itself, with counsel on the new home, the home altar, the home beautiful, good reading at home, forbearance, and the yesterdays of home. The book was meant to be given to a couple on their wedding day. Readers get a Victorian keepsake of vows, advice, and household devotion.
24346-hints-towards-the-formation-of-a-m:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge left this unfinished sketch of a theory of life, edited by Seth B. Watson, of St. John's College and formerly a physician to the Hospital at Oxford, and published in London by John Churchill in 1848. Its contents are a preface, the physiology of life, and the nature of life. Watson thanks Sir John Stoddart, the Reverend James Gillman of Trinity, Lambeth, and Henry Lee, assistant surgeon to King's College Hospital, for kindness toward the publication.

Watson writes that everything from Coleridge's pen bore genius and originality, with comprehensive research and profound meditation. Yet exuberance of imagination and an apparent want of method may leave a first reading unsatisfactory. Coleridge had a method of his own, intelligible to himself, and Watson does not make himself responsible for the speculations. Readers get a fragment of Coleridge thinking about life itself.
24518-memoirs-of-extraordinary-popular-d:
Charles Mackay published the first volume of this famous work at London in 1852, with numerous engravings. It studies the madness of crowds: the schemes, manias, and delusions that sweep whole peoples. The volume opens with the Mississippi Scheme, following John Law from his youth and duel to his escape and his great financial bubble.

Later chapters treat other bubbles, crusades, witch manias, and popular follies, showing how clever people can be carried away together. Mackay quotes Boileau: all men are fools, differing only in degree. His book remains the classic study of financial mania and mass belief, quoted whenever a new bubble bursts.
24683-nan-sherwood-at-palm-beach-or-stra:
Annie Roe Carr wrote this girls' adventure, published at New York by George Sully, as part of the Nan Sherwood series. Earlier volumes took Nan to Pine Camp, Lakeview Hall, winter holidays, and Rose Ranch. This one takes her to Palm Beach, for strange adventures among the orange groves.

Nan, a spirited and loyal heroine, meets new friends, old rivals, and a mystery among the palms and groves of Florida. Carr's tale mixes holiday fun with suspense, in the style girls loved in the 1920s. Young readers get a sunny, old-fashioned adventure, full of Florida sunshine and Nan's good sense.
25604-a-manual-of-the-malay-language-wit:
William Edward Maxwell, barrister of the Inner Temple and assistant resident in Perak, writes this manual of the Malay language, in an eighth edition from Kegan Paul in 1907. An introductory sketch treats the Sanskrit element in Malay.

Maxwell draws on sixteen years of service in Penang, Province Wellesley, Malacca, Singapore, and Perak, teaching the Malay of the British Settlements in the Straits of Malacca. He warns that dialect marks vary by place, so that words common in Penang may sound strange in Malacca, and Kedah speech differs from Patani and Trengganu.
25905-the-100-prize-essay-on-the-cultiva:
The one hundred dollar prize essay on growing the potato, offered by W. T. Wylie in the fall of 1868, fills this small illustrated book from Orange Judd and Company. A committee of farm writers, led by Colonel Mason C. Weld of the American Agriculturist, judged the entries and gave the prize to the winning essay on potato culture. Professor Blot adds a companion piece on how to cook the potato.

The essay takes up soil and its preparation, manuring with green crops, choice of kinds, the effect of soil on seedlings, and how to cross kinds. Practical warnings run through it: a few hours of strong sun ruins the best potato, turning it green and bitter and unfit to eat. Stored spuds should sweat in straw covered field heaps before they go to the cellar, safe from light.
26438-are-the-effects-of-use-and-disuse-:
William Platt Ball's 1890 essay in the Nature Series asks whether habits gained by use, or lost by disuse, pass to children. Spencer and Darwin both kept some remnant of Lamarck's doctrine, by which the inherited effect of habit aided evolution. Ball, helped by Francis Darwin, E. B. Poulton, and Professor Romanes, concludes that acquired characters are not inherited.

His evidence includes birdsong, which nestlings learn from parents rather than inherit, even when they pick up another species' song and teach it onward. Dogs, he argues, do not inherit intelligence gained by living with humans. Weismann, Wallace, and Galton stand with Ball against use-inheritance, and the essay weighs its social import as well as its biology.
2704-washington-and-his-comrades-in-arms:
George M. Wrong wrote this chronicle of Washington and his comrades for the Chronicles of America series, volume 12 in the Abraham Lincoln edition. Wrong owns a certain audacity in taking on so great a subject, and his preface meets it with modesty.

The book follows Washington through the War of Independence, with Greene, Knox, Lafayette, and the other comrades who held an army together. Wrong writes for general readers, clear and fair, with the politics never far from the battles. The chronicle serves as a sound one volume guide to the Revolution's leaders.
27322-an-appeal-to-the-british-nation-on:
Sir William Hillary, Baronet, published this appeal in London in 1825, in a third edition, calling for a national institution to preserve lives and property from shipwreck. He dedicates the work to the King, ruler of the world's greatest sea power. He writes with the urgency of a man who has watched storms scatter ruin along the coasts.

Hillary argues both the humanity and the policy of the plan: saving shipwrecked sailors is a moral duty, and a maritime nation gains by doing it well. His earlier writings on steam lifeboats and fire at sea stand behind the case. The pamphlet is a founding document of organized lifeboat rescue in Britain.
29086-the-mushroom-edible-and-otherwise-:
M. E. Hard, superintendent of public instruction at Kirkwood, Missouri, wrote this 1908 guide, The Mushroom, Edible and Otherwise, published by the Mushroom Publishing Company of Columbus, Ohio. The book gives the habitat and time of growth of nearly all common species, with photographic pictures, as a guide to studying mushrooms, with special reference to edible and poisonous varieties.

Hard dedicates it to his wife, whose knowledge of plant life and patience in preserving fungal specimens, scattered from back porch to library, helped the work throughout. A note in memoriam honors Dr. W. A. Kellerman, who died still seeking wider knowledge of nature. Readers get a classic American mushroom guide, useful for identification and caution alike, with plates from original specimens.
29145-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-r:
Henry Cabot Lodge and Francis W. Halsey edited this tenth volume of The Best of the World's Classics, Restricted to Prose, published by Funk and Wagnalls in 1909. Volume ten covers America, part two, from 1807 to 1909, and adds an index to all ten volumes. The series gathered the best prose of the world with introductions and biographical notes.

Contents include Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Edgar Allan Poe, Oliver Wendell Holmes, Margaret Fuller, Horace Greeley, and John Lothrop Motley. Poe appears with The Cask of Amontillado and his essays on Hawthorne and the short story. Readers get a generous anthology of American prose, useful for sampling major writers in short, well-chosen pieces.
2926-a-critical-examination-of-the-posit:
Thomas Henry Huxley delivered this critical examination of Darwin's Origin of Species as the closing lecture of his series on organic nature. He reviews the facts and reasonings from five earlier lectures, reminding listeners that his quotations from Darwin served as data rather than theory. The question now is where Darwin's work stands within a complete theory of the causes of organic change.

Huxley tests the idea of gradual modification, noting that a creature descended from an elephant-like mammal should resemble an elephant, and one from an armadillo-like mammal should resemble an armadillo. On that supposition the facts become intelligible, he argues, and on any other they do not. The lecture shows Huxley the advocate at his most disciplined, separating evidence from speculation.
30265-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-15-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for March 1865, volume 15, number 89, leads with The Story of a Year, a Civil War romance from Ticknor and Fields. Its narrator notes that many stories of the last three years begin as his does, and end when the hero is despatched, since romance stops where a hero falls. In early May, two years before, a young couple strolled homeward from an evening walk among peaceful hills enclosing their rustic home.

Into those hills the young man brought not rumor but a whiff of gunpowder and the clank of a sword, for Mr. John Ford, his campaign still before him, wore the comely air of camp life. Villagers took him for a very Hector, Miss Elizabeth Crowe for a very pretty fellow, and his fresh lieutenant's blue and gold shone strange in happy Northern glades. The number mixes war, love, and letters in the Atlantic manner.
30470-the-winning-of-popular-government-:
Archibald MacMechan writes The Winning of Popular Government, a chronicle of the Union of 1841, published in Toronto in 1916 and dedicated to Robert Alexander Falconer of the University of Toronto. A frontispiece shows the burning of the Parliament Buildings in Montreal in 1849, from a drawing by C. W. Jefferys.

Five chapters move from Durham the dictator and Poulett Thomson the peacemaker to reform in the saddle, the great administration, and the principle established. An epilogue, bibliographical note, and index close the volume. MacMechan tells how Canada won responsible government, in a clear chronicle for general readers and students.
30611-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-15-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly, volume fifteen, number ninety, for April 1865, presents a magazine of literature, art, and politics, entered for copyright in 1865 by Ticknor and Fields of Boston. Its opening piece, Adventures of a Lone Woman, begins with Miselle declaring she will go and see the oil.

Caleb lays the Morning Journal on the table and calmly accepts whatever new dispensation Providence and Miselle have allotted him. Asked if she means whaling, Miselle answers no, she means the Oil Springs, lying in the remotest portion of Pennsylvania. The issue captures Civil War era America in fiction, essays, and comment, at a moment of national change.
30961-the-rushton-boys-at-rally-hall-or-:
Spencer Davenport, author of The Rushton Boys in the Saddle and At Treasure Cove, wrote this boys' book. It was published by Whitman Publishing in Racine, Wisconsin, with copyright in 1916 by George Sully and Company. Its full title promises great days in school and out at Rally Hall. Thirty chapters carry the Rushton boys from home to school and through a year of scrapes and games.

Early chapters include A Rash Impulse, The Runaway, A Narrow Escape, Facing the Music, Uncle Aaron Rages, Teddy's Banishment, The Missing Papers, A Fruitless Search, Chasing the Tramps, and Bunk Goes Crazy. They end with The Robbery. Later chapters bring Off for Rally Hall, Andy Shanks the bully, Hardtack Rally, Learning the Ropes, A Jolly Crowd, Teddy's Joke, Kicking the Pigskin, and The Man with the Scar. It is a lively school story for boys.
31345-history-of-the-intellectual-develo:
John William Draper's History of the Intellectual Development of Europe appears here in a revised edition in two volumes. This is volume one, entered for copyright in 1876 by Harper and Brothers of New York. Draper was professor of chemistry at the University of New York. He sets out to trace how European thought developed from age to age, treating intellectual history as a story with laws and stages rather than a string of separate thinkers.

The volume's preface links the work to the British Association for the Advancement of Science, and its chapters move through the ancient and medieval worlds toward modern Europe. Readers will find a sweeping, nineteenth-century synthesis, confident in science and in progress. Later scholars have challenged Draper's scheme, but the book's ambition and range still make it a landmark of Victorian intellectual history.
32204-hungarian-sketches-in-peace-and-wa:
Hungarian Sketches in Peace and War, translated from the Hungarian of Moritz Jokai with a prefatory notice by Emeric Szabad, was published in Edinburgh, London, and Dublin in 1854. It forms volume one of Constable's Miscellany of Foreign Literature. Szabad, author of Hungary Past and Present, presents Jokai as one of the most popular Hungarian prose writers of fiction to spring up a few years before the late war. He is praised for wit, fluent style, and vivid pictures of Hungarian life as it stood.

Its contents run from Dear Relations and The Bardy Family through Crazy Marcsa, Comorn, Mor Perczel, and Gergely Sonkolyi. They continue to The Unlucky Weathercock, The Two Brides, The Brewer, The Szekely Mother, and A Ball. Readers get mid-nineteenth-century Hungarian stories of peace and war, family, soldiers, and village life, in a flowing translation for British readers.
32350-noteworthy-records-of-bats-from-ni:
J. Knox Jones junior, James Dale Smith, and Ronald W. Turner report bat records from Nicaragua in Occasional Papers of the Museum of Natural History at the University of Kansas, number 2, dated April 29, 1971. Nicaragua, they note, sits in a key spot for Central American mammal patterns, yet little had been published on its fauna. Their paper records distribution, variation, and natural history for forty species of bats, fourteen recorded from the country for the first time.

Most specimens came from field parties working in Nicaragua in 1964, 1966, 1967, and 1968, with earlier material from 1956. An appended checklist cites only primary literature that refers to actual specimens from Nicaragua. The paper suits readers in mammalogy, ecology, and Central American natural history who need solid, specimen-based records.
32821-the-picturesque-antiquities-of-spa:
Nathaniel Armstrong Wells describes the antiquities of Spain in a series of letters, published in London by Richard Bentley in 1846. Illustrations show Moorish palaces, cathedrals, and other monuments in Burgos, Valladolid, Toledo, and Seville.

Wells writes plainly, avoiding technical terms, and hopes to pioneer a path for a more scientific pen. His visits came after revolution had stripped church processions of their splendor, leaving stone and marble where color once crowded. Letters from Seville, though placed last, date from an earlier tour. Toledo brings the fable of Hercules and his cavern, and a Moorish sailor with curious scruples about killing poultry.
32994-the-marvelous-exploits-of-paul-bun:
W. B. Laughead's collection gathers the tall tales of Paul Bunyan as told in the camps of the white pine lumbermen. The stories were handed down for generations while loggers pioneered the north woods from Maine to California. The Red River Lumber Company published the book for the amusement of its friends. The book calls Bunyan America's only myth, a hero of lumbercamp whoppers told to awe greenhorns in the bunkhouse and strangers in the saloon.

Laughead collected the tales from various sources and embellished them for print, with illustrations including Paul and his big blue ox. The stories were never told as straight narrative in camp, he notes, but dropped casually as if they were common knowledge. That casual exaggeration is the joke and the art: a lumberman who could reshape a landscape becomes, in these pages, a national folk hero.
33172-down-town-brooklyn-a-report-to-the:
Down Town Brooklyn, a report to the Comptroller of the City of New York dated 1913, addresses sites for public buildings. It also covers the relocation of elevated railroad tracks in lower Fulton Street, Brooklyn. A letter from the comptroller dated April 18, 1913, argues that the time has arrived for a definite policy on needed improvements in Brooklyn. It refers in particular to settling court house, bridge terminal, and other questions, after much discussion that produced divergent views.

The report that follows, with committee reports, first through sixth plans, an additional report, and a supplemental report, weighs where courts, terminals, and tracks should go in a growing borough. Its maps and plans show a city trying to order its center before growth forced its hand. For historians of New York planning, the volume is a detailed record of how Brooklyn's downtown was debated, and of the choices that shaped it.
33507-the-mammals-of-washtenaw-county-mi:
Norman A. Wood's Mammals of Washtenaw County, Michigan, published in July 1922 as number 123 of the University of Michigan's Occasional Papers, surveys the county's mammals. Wood notes three natural divisions crossing the county from northwest to southeast, with a rough moraine of loose soil in the northwest. His paper maps where mammals live, in a county of farms, woods, and waters.

The paper suits readers of Michigan natural history, offering a short, factual census of a county's wild mammals. Its tone is precise and field-based, aimed at naturalists and students. For local historians and biologists, it is a useful baseline, showing what lived in Washtenaw County a century ago.
33816-the-hollow-tree-and-deep-woods-boo:
Albert Bigelow Paine gathered two earlier books into this one volume, with new stories and pictures by J. M. Conde added. The Hollow Tree and In the Deep Woods tell animal tales for children, set among woodland folk who live, talk, and get into scrapes much like people. An invitation from Jack Rabbit opens the set.

Young readers meet creatures of field and wood in short, gentle tales meant for reading aloud. Paine, later known for his life of Mark Twain, writes in a warm, simple voice. The book endures as a cozy woodland storybook, best read slowly, one tale at a time.
3704-journal-of-researches-into-the-natu:
Charles Darwin writes the journal of his voyage on HMS Beagle, covering the natural history and geology of the countries visited during the years 1832 to 1836. The volume, reprinted many times from 1874 to 1913, opens with an illustration of the Beagle in the Straits of Magellan, with Mount Sarmiento in the distance. Darwin describes South America, the Galapagos, Australia, and the long voyage home.

The journal records birds, beasts, fossils, rocks, and peoples with the curiosity that later shaped On the Origin of Species. Readers meet a young naturalist learning to see a world in change. The book suits anyone who wants Darwin before he became famous, traveling, collecting, and thinking aloud on a ship bound around the world.
4089-the-american-nation-a-history-volum:
E. P. Cheyney's history opens the American Nation series with the European background of American history. A chapter on Italian contributions to exploration from 1200 to 1500 notes that Italy, having lost commercial leadership, stayed the teacher of Europe.

In the arts at the base of exploration, as in many other fields, Italy stood far ahead of other western lands, preserving ancient skill through the Middle Ages. Cheyney traces maps, ships, and learning from Europe to America. Readers who like clear, scholarly surveys will find a solid first volume for the whole series.
4334-observations-on-the-effects-of-the-:
The Reverend T. R. Malthus, professor of political economy at the East India College, published these observations in London in 1814. Parliament was about to revise the corn laws. Malthus urged that so great a decision rest on a sound grasp of the entire question.

The stability of the measures, and their effects, depended on getting the question right. He examines how a rise or fall in the price of corn affects farming. He examines how it affects the general wealth of the country. The pamphlet is short, topical, and practical, written to inform a live debate. It shows Malthus the economist at work on policy, rather than on population theory.
5800-the-marvelous-exploits-of-paul-buny:
Laughead collects the marvelous exploits of Paul Bunyan as told in the camps of the White Pine lumbermen for generations. Loggers pioneered the way through the north woods from Maine to California. They carried Bunyan tales with them, the text explains. Laughead gathered these from various sources and embellished them for publication, with text and illustrations. The result is a lumberjack mythology in print.

We meet a giant logger whose feats explain lakes, rivers, and forests, told in tall-tale style with a straight face. The book suits children, folklorists, and lovers of American tall tales, since it preserves camp humor alongside heroic exaggeration. It remains the classic printed source for Bunyan, and a delightful entry to how working men turned labor into legend.
9389-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-05-no-2:
In March 1860, the Atlantic Monthly, a Boston magazine of writing, art, and public affairs, printed its twenty-ninth issue. Like other issues of the day, it mixes essays, tales, and book notices in one volume. The lead piece takes up the French character, as seen through American eyes. Later pages turn to screw propulsion for ships and to plain descriptive prose.

The French essay tracks how Americans formed their views of France, from stage jokes and novels to Lafayette and the Revolution. The ship piece weighs a new way to drive vessels through water. Reviews at the back size up fresh American books. A reader gets a firm sense of what sharp mid-century readers argued about, from foreign nations to new machines.
9396-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-05-no-3:
The April 1860 issue of the Atlantic Monthly opens with an essay called The Laws of Beauty. It asks what makes a form or a face fair to the eye, and answers that beauty springs from mind, not mere matter. The same number prints a short tale called An Experience, a piece about thieves, and verse on bardic signs. Reviews of new books close the issue, as was the custom.

Beauty, the lead essay claims, shows thought and law made plain in shape, from carved marble to a plain curve. The tales and poems beside it test the same theme in life: risk, wrong, and old song. A reader gets a lively sample of 1860 taste, where art theory, story, and book talk sat side by side.
961-glinda-of-oz-in-which-are-related-th:
L. Frank Baum wrote this Oz tale of Princess Ozma and Dorothy, on a hazardous journey to the home of the Flatheads and to the Magic Isle of the Skeezers. The two friends face dire peril on the isle, and only the sorcery of Glinda the Good, the sorceress of the South, can rescue them.

Baum, Royal Historian of Oz, tells the quest with his usual wit and wonder, as Ozma's wisdom and Dorothy's pluck meet strange peoples and magics. Glinda's arrival turns the tide, and the tale ends in peace. The book, the last Oz tale Baum wrote, is a fitting farewell to his fairy land.
9661-mormon-settlement-in-arizona-a-reco:
James H. McClintock, Arizona historian, wrote Mormon Settlement in Arizona in 1921, a record of peaceful conquest of the desert. The book tells how Mormon pioneers broke the wilderness, farmed new lands, and built towns across Arizona. Early chapters follow the Mormon Battalion's march through the Southwest, past Tucson toward California. Later chapters map towns, place names, and frontier trials.

McClintock draws on journals, march records, and pioneer tales, with photos of leaders and crossings. The story stresses farming, order, and endurance over strife. A reader gets a detailed settler history of Arizona, told by a historian close to the pioneers' own records.
9997-france-and-england-in-north-america:
Francis Parkman's third volume in his France and England in North America series tells how the Great West, the valleys of the Mississippi and the Lakes, was revealed to the world. Parkman, writing in 1870, calls the region's early story obscure, its motives and incidents barely known.

Chapters follow Cavelier de La Salle, the Sulpitians and Jesuits on the lakes, France taking possession of the West, and the discovery of the Mississippi, with Frontenac behind the enterprise. Parkman writes narrative history with a novelist's eye. Readers get exploration, rivalry, and endurance on a continental scale.
a-book-for-all-readers-an-aid-to-the-col:
A Book for All Readers, published in 1900 by Ainsworth Rand Spofford, is a practical guide to books and libraries. Its full subtitle states its program: an aid to the collection, use, and preservation of books, and to the formation of public and private libraries. Spofford wrote as a leading American librarian of his generation, and the book carries that professional authority.

Inside, readers find counsel on choosing books, building a collection, and caring for it so it lasts. The guidance serves both the private buyer forming a home library and the citizen helping to found a public one. It remains a period manual of librarianship, showing how Americans around 1900 were taught to gather, organize, and preserve their books.
a-critical-examination-of-the-position-o:
Thomas Henry Huxley delivered this lecture to working men at the Museum of Practical Geology in 1863, as the title states, the sixth of six lectures on the causes of organic change. He begins by noting how often he has quoted Darwin's famous book on facts, never on theory. Now he weighs Darwin's own argument directly.

Huxley asks what a complete theory of species would require, then measures natural selection against that standard with care. He defends Darwin's method and honesty while marking where proof still falls short. The lecture shows Darwin's great champion at his fairest: clear, bold, and exact, speaking science to a working audience without talking down.
a-narrative-of-the-life-and-adventures-o: Venture Smith tells his own life story in this brief narrative, from capture in Africa at eight years old to more than sixty years of residence in the United States. Brought to America enslaved and denied schooling, he recounts labour, family, and the slow effort to purchase his freedom. The preface presents the account as simple fact, vouched for by people living who knew most of what he relates.
a-narrative-of-the-most-remarkable-parti: James Albert Ukawsaw Gronniosaw, an African prince, relates his life and spiritual experience in this narrative taken from his own mouth and set down by a young lady of Leominster. Dedicated to the Countess of Huntingdon, the account traces his passage from Africa into slavery and toward Christian faith. It presents his story as evidence of divine dealings with him. The preface notes the account was first taken down for a lady's private satisfaction before reaching print.
discourse-on-criticism-and-of-poetry-fro:
A verse essay on criticism fills Samuel Cobb's discourse, drawn from his Poems on Several Occasions of 1707. The Augustan Reprint Society issued this copy in July 1946, as number one of its second series, with an introduction by Louis I. Bredvold. The piece is cast as a letter to Richard Carter, late of the Middle Temple and then living in Barbados.

Cobb's full head names it a discourse on criticism and the liberty of writing. The Muses, daughters of memory, head his plea to a far-off friend. Verse then praises Rome's Cicero and a great Johnson, whose deeds stand parallel with Macedon's hero. Learning the victor's language is a theme. The piece shows Augustan critics at work in rhyme.
doe-osti-17152722-dissertation-proposal-:
Emma Rudziensky's dissertation proposal, issued by Los Alamos on 5 October 2026, plans a hunt for better solid materials for Cherenkov detectors. Cherenkov light flashes when a fast charged particle outruns light inside a material. Detectors using that flash serve treaty checks, medicine, physics, pulsed power, and materials work. Fused silica is the usual light source solid, and the study aims to beat it.

Candidate solids include sapphire and heavy metal fluoride glasses. Planned tests cover how each solid passes light and how it glows under rays, heat, and excitation. Results would feed response models for each candidate, and the solids would be ranked for detector use. The top pick then anchors a detector module design with tuned light collection, tested in the MCNP6 code. An AI usage note discloses ChatGPT help with the writing.
doe-osti-1740015-first-arm-mobile-facili:
Brookhaven National Laboratory handbook DOE/SC-ARM-TR-263, by J Uin, S Smith, and O Mayol-Bracero in May 2026, documents the aerosol observing system of the first ARM Mobile Facility. The system, called AOS01, packs a full suite of particle instruments into a mobile laboratory that the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement program deploys to field campaigns. A shared inlet on the roof feeds sampled air to the racks inside.

The suite spans instruments that count and size particles, measure their chemistry, and test how they take up water or seed cloud droplets. Named units include a scanning mobility particle sizer, an aerodynamic particle sizer, a soot photometer, nephelometers, and a cloud condensation nuclei counter. Handbook sections cover the mentor and vendor contacts, the inlet and enclosure hardware, the measurements taken, and how the data products are organized for users.
doe-osti-2583514-research-development-an:
CRADA final report NREL/TP-5400-94490, dated April 1, 2025, closes one of NREL's longest umbrellas: CRD-01-00098, an agreement dating to 2001 with the South Coast Air Quality Management District. Kenneth Kelly was the laboratory's contact. Under it, the partners ran joint research, development, and demonstration projects to push alternative fuels into the real marketplace, modification after modification, for over two decades.

The founding project field-tested a small vehicle fleet on Fischer-Tropsch synthetic diesel, a clean-burning fuel made from gas rather than crude. West Virginia University measured the fleet's emissions under a separate subcontract. Later modifications stacked further clean-fuel vehicle projects onto the same frame, and the report walks them in the order they were added. Few CRADAs live this long. The document functions as a compact history of how alternative fuel demonstration actually happened: one fleet, one fuel, one air district at a time.
doe-osti-2587115-environmentally-friendl:
William Easter and Bruce Mutter led this final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-FE0031985, submitted in December 2024 and revised in August 2025. Their company, X-MAT CCC, tested building materials made largely from coal-derived carbon, using technology licensed from Semplastics. The project ran from January 2021 through November 2024.

The products, sold under names such as X-BRIX, X-PANEL, X-MATRIX, and X-TILES, hold at least 52 percent coal-derived carbon by mass. Counting the carbon in the resin binders, the total carbon share reaches at least 71 percent. The team built a prototype demonstrator structure, produced a detailed design for a carbon-based building, and updated its techno-economic analysis with market surveys. A gap analysis and a life-cycle analysis of the materials accompany the report. The aim is a new, high-volume use for carbon ore that keeps the carbon locked in solid products.
doe-osti-2588250-technoeconomic-prefeasi:
Ben Ollis of Oak Ridge National Laboratory wrote this prefeasibility study, ORNL/TM-2025/4132, dated August 2025. It asks what energy resources a facility in Punta Gorda, Florida, could place behind its meter, on its own side of the utility connection. Solar generation anchors the options, with three candidate sites identified on the property.

The three solar sites measure 42, 44, and 18 acres. For the analysis they are treated as one large array rather than several small ones. The facility plans to expand soon, but the study notes the expansion should leave these sites untouched. Prefeasibility here means screening economics before committing to design. The study weighs the resources technoeconomically, matching generation to the site's needs and costs. The framing pairs energy supply with resilience, the ability to keep a facility running through grid trouble, which matters in hurricane country.
doe-osti-2997329-catalytic-water-splitti:
The first steps of splitting water with light and catalysts are studied by Alec Talin, Thomas Chan, and David Chandler, in Sandia report SAND2025-12160 dated September 2025. Solar water splitting could make hydrogen fuel from sunlight, but the opening molecular moves are hard to watch. One chapter films a manganese carbonyl compound breaking apart under light, both free in gas and sitting on a surface.

Velocity map imaging records the speed and direction of the carbon monoxide fragments thrown off. Spectra were integrated over chosen image areas and plotted against time delay after the light flash. Modeled signals followed the general trend of the measured ones. Kinetics at this scale tell catalyst designers which bonds break first, and how a surface changes the story, before they scale a reactor.
doe-osti-2997796-transverse-spin-and-mom:
Pennsylvania State University final technical report on award DE-FG02-07ER41460, by Leonard Gamberg, closes a long research line running from November 2006 to June 2025. The subject is the three-dimensional spin and momentum structure of hadrons, the protons and other particles built from quarks and gluons. Deep-inelastic scattering experiments probe that structure by smashing electrons into targets.

The report explains the split at the heart of the field. At short distances quarks interact weakly and can be computed. Long-distance behavior is packed into correlation functions that experiments must measure. Highlights include global fits for transverse single-spin asymmetries and the nucleon tensor charges checked against the Soffer bound. A 2023 study of lambda particle polarization, in electron-positron annihilation and in scattering planned for the Electron-Ion Collider, is among the results gathered. The volume caps nearly two decades of theory work.
doe-osti-3002220-operational-and-perform:
T. J. Mathews, R. T. Jett, N. A. Griffiths, and a large Oak Ridge team report a year of pond monitoring in ORNL/TM-2025/4096, dated September 2025. The ponds sit at the East Tennessee Technology Park, the former K-25 uranium enrichment site. Two ponds, K-1007-P1 and K-901-A, carry a legacy of PCB contamination in their sediment and fish.

Monitoring tracks PCB levels in fish and clams, general water quality, and shoreline and aquatic plants. In the K-1007-P1 pond, PCB levels in sunfish fillets and whole fish now fall below cleanup targets. Largemouth bass levels have dropped tenfold from before remediation. Fish management converted that pond to a community led by low-accumulating species, and grass carp are now scarce. The report serves as the 2025 performance record for the cleanup.
doe-osti-3006181-large-scale-offshore-wi:
Final report DE-SC0023254 from Umberto Ciri at the University of Puerto Rico at Mayaguez studies what large offshore wind farms would do to weather and ocean conditions around Puerto Rico. The island imports fossil fuels and pays more for electricity than the U.S. mainland, while its offshore wind resource is strong. Effects of wind farms on air and ocean circulation had not been studied at tropical latitude before this project.

The project ran the WRF weather model for one year, December 2021 to November 2022, fed by NAM boundary conditions. The wind fields were checked against reanalysis and buoy data, in agreement. Results indicate that wind farm wakes can change wind stress, drive Ekman vertical transport, and possibly shift nutrient distribution. A fully coupled ocean-atmosphere model proved harder than planned; large-eddy simulations carried much of the wake work, and the report leaves coupling as the next step.
doe-osti-3006387-phylogenomic-discovery-:
Final technical report for DOE award DE-SC0018247 closes the NitFix project, which worked to uncover the genetic basis of nitrogen-fixing root nodules and engineer the trait into plants that lack it. The first aim built a phylogeny of roughly 14,000 species across the Rosid I clade, which holds every nodulating lineage. Targeted gene sets were sequenced from herbarium specimens of more than 15,000 species and assembled with a custom pipeline, giving the largest phylogenomic dataset for any plant clade.

Later aims tested nodulation gene function in the legume Medicago and in Populus, a non-nodulating bioenergy crop, and pushed toward engineering nodulation in Populus itself. Listed papers show poplar can perceive lipo-chitooligosaccharide signals, and that a Populus homolog of the NODULE INCEPTION gene positively regulates lateral root formation. The report synthesizes findings across the aims rather than presenting one experiment.
doe-osti-3006496-deployment-and-evaluati:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4190, by Anjus George and dated December 2025, covers SciStream's deployment and evaluation on the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility's Advanced Computing Ecosystem, ACE. SciStream streams data between scientific instruments and computing sites so analysis can keep pace with experiments. The report walks through the architecture and components. A local setup built with Docker follows: starting a consumer application, producer and consumer services, and a user client that sends requests and streams data.

Deployment ran on the Olivine OpenShift cluster. The evaluation sections weigh platform limits that shape the design, among them NodePorts. External access through them needs extra firewall rules. The dynamic port range SciStream wants is only supported in newer Kubernetes versions. Future OLCF policy may disallow NodePorts entirely, since their traffic is hard to inspect. The author warns against building SciStream to depend heavily on NodePorts until Istio-based routing is in place.
doe-osti-3008763-queued-up-2025-edition-:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's Queued Up: 2025 Edition is the annual census of power plants waiting to connect to the American transmission grid. Joseph Rand, Nick Manderlink, Steven Zhang, and seven co-authors compiled it. The data run through the end of 2024 and come from transmission providers' public interconnection queues.

The slide-format report counts queued capacity region by region. PJM alone lists 4,885 projects totalling 580.2 gigawatts, and the non-ISO West lists 4,871 projects at 856.9 gigawatts. Tables separate active, operational, and withdrawn projects so readers can see how little of the queue historically gets built. The authors present trends without recommending policy.
doe-osti-3009800-multidimensional-cohere:
Multidimensional coherent spectroscopy of van der Waals materials is covered by Michigan's Steven Cundiff in a final report for DOE award DE-SC0022179, spanning August 2021 to December 2024. The samples are monolayer semiconductors such as MoSe2 and WSe2, one atom thick.

Double-quantum spectroscopy picks out signals that come only from interactions, showing biexcitons and exciton-trion correlations hidden in ordinary spectra. Electrical gating tuned carrier populations inside boron nitride-encapsulated samples while tests ran. Paired imaging mapped how strain, wrinkles, and charge puddles spread exciton energies across a flake, the disorder that otherwise blurs every coherent reading.
doe-osti-3011645-how-snow-drives-the-sea:
Snow cover controls spring albedo across the Alaskan high Arctic coast in the final report for award DE-SC0019107 by Jennifer Delamere and Matthew Sturm of the University of Alaska Fairbanks. The SALVO field campaign observed tundra and sea ice near Utqiagvik during the 2019, 2022, and 2024 melt seasons. Fully snow covered ground reflects at broadband albedo near 0.8, while snow free tundra or ponded ice sits near 0.15.

Three sites covered the ARM facility, a Barrow Environmental Observatory line, and Elson Lagoon sea ice. Snow depth was measured at one metre intervals and albedo at five metre intervals, nearly daily from mid April to mid June. Wind, not snowfall, proved the prime agent shaping snow distribution, giving repeatable melt patterns year to year.
doe-osti-3011891-thermodynamic-profiling:
Thermodynamic profiles of the atmosphere come from infrared spectra in a National Renewable Energy Laboratory guide by Stefano Letizia, Vincent Michaud-Belleau of LR Tech, David Turner of NOAA, and Aliza Abraham. The ASSIST spectrometer supplies the readings, and the TROPoe algorithm does the retrievals. Three foundations shape the guide: spectrometry, radiative transfer, and optimal estimation.

Instrument limits get full treatment: radiometric calibration, finite optical path length, sampling rate, detector nonlinearity, and field of view. Worked case studies show how profile data are read and checked before use. For weakly nonlinear forward models, error bars follow the linear case at convergence.
doe-osti-3012535-direct-solar-self-catal:
Fisher, Timothy Scott, principal investigator at UCLA, led this final technical report, dated December 30, 2025, for award DE-FE0032354. Working with Southwest Solar Technology and SolGrapH, the team built a way to split natural gas into hydrogen fuel and solid graphite using concentrated sunlight. The process, called solar thermal pyrolysis, cracks methane with heat instead of burning it, so no carbon dioxide is released.

The team designed, built, and ran a field-scale reactor under real sun. Tests showed sunlight could decompose natural gas at pilot scale, locking the carbon away as a saleable solid rather than a greenhouse gas. Laser sensors fitted into the exhaust line measured the gas mix during runs. The report also covers cost analysis and student training tied to the project.
doe-osti-3012856-characterization-of-org:
Haofei Zhang of the University of California, Riverside, wrote this ARM field campaign report, DOE/SC-ARM-26-003, dated January 2026. The campaign profiled organosulfates and organonitrates. These are two families of organic aerosol particles. Crews sampled them at set heights above the Southern Great Plains site in Oklahoma. Ground studies had found them in a large share of organic aerosol mass. Their pattern with height was still poorly known.

All 157 samples were run through high-resolution mass spectrometry at the Environmental Molecular Sciences Laboratory. Of the samples, 52 came from aircraft and 105 from the ground. Early comparisons left the height trends unclear. Fuller statistical work is under way. The stakes are plain: aerosols are still the largest single source of doubt in Earth's radiation balance.
doe-osti-3013133-high-accuracy-and-high-:
Ming Han of Michigan State University led this final technical report for award DE-FE0031899, submitted January 15, 2026, on fiber-optic temperature sensors for coal-fired advanced energy systems. Power plant parts run far too hot for ordinary electronics, so the team built sensors from glass fiber that read temperature from reflected light. The performance window ran from room temperature to over 800 degrees Celsius.

One design uses an air-filled Fabry-Perot cavity, a tiny mirrored gap in the fiber, whose pressure can be adjusted through a side-hole fiber. Changing the pressure tunes the sensor's response. The report covers fabrication, noise analysis, and characterization tests, plus a second cavity design built in a silica tube. Such sensors could monitor turbines and boilers where wiring cannot survive.
doe-osti-3016249-hydrodynamic-analysis-a:
Thanh Toan Tran, Stein Housner, and Will Wiley were the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contacts for this January 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-5700-97259. The subject is the Aquantis AQ10, a floating axial-flow tidal turbine with a tri-cat mooring layout, as the design terms it. The aim was to predict its water performance and dynamic loads more accurately.

The team checked simpler reduced-order models against high-fidelity simulations.
