One comparison ran the turbine alone at rated conditions: an inflow current of 2.1 meters per second and a rotor speed of 24 revolutions per minute. The RAFT response toolbox, expanded for marine turbines under the SHARKS program, plus an optimizer, explored platform size and mooring layout choices. Turbine designers get faster models they can trust for the next design round.
doe-osti-3018185-quantum-enabled-precisi:
David Leibrandt of the University of California Los Angeles led this report for award DE-SC0021368, submitted February 14, 2026. Jun Ye, Sae Woo Nam, and Joel Ullom were co-investigators. The period ran from September 2020 to August 2023. The target was the thorium-229 nuclear isomer transition, a clock tick that could one day out-measure atomic clocks.

At project start, the best transition energies were 7.8 and 8.28 electronvolts with wide error bars. The team aimed to cut uncertainty to ten millielectronvolts using calorimetry: catch the decay energy with superconducting nanowire detectors. They built a buffer gas stopping cell at the University of Colorado to harvest thorium-229 from uranium-233 decay as ions. In the end they detected thorium ions with a channel plate detector, but saw no signal in the nanowire detectors. The report names the two causes plainly: too few ions delivered, and too small a detector.
doe-osti-3018336-feasibility-and-strateg:
Iyabo Usman, Nicolas Stauff, and Temitope Taiwo of Argonne National Laboratory wrote this report, ANL/NSE-26/3, on deploying nuclear power reactors in Africa. Many African states want firm, low-carbon power for industrial parks and coastal cities, and vendors are courting them. The report tests feasibility country by country, then draws out the strategic implications for the continent and for supplier nations.

Each country case balances promise against named risks. Ghana's program, for example, is driven by clear national intent. The recurring risk list is blunt: tariff affordability, thin regulatory capacity in newcomer states, and project bankability against cheaper geothermal and renewable options. Flexibility alongside renewables counts as a nuclear strength. The audience is decision makers on both sides of these deals. The report gives them a shared, unsentimental fact base before contracts get signed.
doe-osti-3018766-feasibility-analyses-fo:
Anjan Debnath and Timothy McJunkin of Idaho National Laboratory, with Jimmy E Quiroz, Melissa Louie, and Rachid Darbali-Zamora of Sandia, studied a mountain microgrid in SAND2026-16656R, January 2026. The client is the Cooperativa Hidroelectrica de la Montana, an electric cooperative in Puerto Rico's Cordillera Central. Its towns are Adjuntas, Jayuya, Lares, Maricao, and Utuado. The work ran under the Communities Local Energy Action Program. Four studies examine different aspects of distributed energy development for the region.

Mountain terrain shapes every answer: roads, loads, and hazards differ from the coast. The analyses used tools such as ReNCAT to rate how hard facilities are to serve and reach. Cell towers, grocery stores, and services were scored for criticality and effort. Feasibility here means matching solar, storage, and hydro resources to a cooperative's real map. The report gives the cooperative and DOE a staged basis for investment decisions.
doe-osti-3023600-direct-vitrification-of:
Keith S Matlack, I Joseph, Ian L Pegg, and Wing K Kot of the Vitreous State Laboratory at the Catholic University of America. They evaluated which Hanford tanks could feed direct vitrification of high-level waste. Their report VSL-19R4470-1, Revision 0, was published in February 2020 for the Department of Energy's environmental management office in Richland, Washington. Direct vitrification would turn tank waste into glass without some of the usual pretreatment steps.

Tank-by-tank tables test washed and unwashed waste fractions and list what crystals form, since crystals such as nepheline, spinel, and sulfate phases can spoil glass quality. For tank BX-101, a one-third washed sample reached about 41 percent loading with nepheline noted, while BX-102 fractions ran higher. The screening gives planners a ranked view of source tanks.
doe-osti-3024312-low-temperature-plasma-: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and SirenOpt Inc. closed CRADA FP00017649 with this final summary, report LBNL-2001753, dated March 19, 2026, with Melanie Sonsteng as lab contact and Jared O'Leary for the company. Under Cyclotron Road, sponsored by Activate, SirenOpt tested a low-temperature plasma sensor. It measures key properties of lithium-ion battery electrode material in real time on the production line. The summary argues that catching bad electrodes early matters, because vehicle makers add up to ten percent extra cells as insurance against weak ones. It lists no publications or inventions.
doe-osti-3363258-smartgrid-advanced-load:
Portland General Electric closes out award DE-EE0009778 with this final report on the SALMON project. Rick Hodges and Matt Hubbard led the work. The project ran from June 2022 to October 2025. It sat in the Solar Energy Technologies Office's Connected Communities program. Its goal was to show the value of distributed energy resources as a grid resource. That value spans both bulk system and distribution operations.

The team built project management systems and held a June 2022 kickoff. It also wrote an evaluation plan and survey instruments. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory guided that work for the whole cohort. A no cost time extension came first. DOE then terminated the award on October 3, 2025. The report records the work status at that point.
doe-osti-3365150-sup-230-sup-th-sup-234-:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-24157, by Allison Wende, Rebecca Foley, Zsuzsanna Macsik, and seven co-authors, dates an International Atomic Energy Agency environmental sample. Cotton swipe 27107-14-04, received November 3, 2025, was age-dated with the thorium-230/uranium-234 radiochronometer, which reads how long ago the uranium was last chemically purified. The work supports nuclear safeguards inspections.

Standard preparation ashed the swipes, but 2025 tests showed the cotton itself carries nanogram levels of thorium-232 and femtogram levels of thorium-230, enough to corrupt the clock. A new method isolates sample material without leaching the cotton. Uranium was measured by isotope dilution mass spectrometry in December 2025, with detection limits of 275 and 480 femtograms for uranium-235 and uranium-238. Thorium aliquots were spiked with about 3 picograms of thorium-229 tracer and purified on ion exchange columns.
doe-osti-3375831-collaborative-research-:
The final technical report for Department of Energy grant DE-SC0019346, dated June 28, 2026, closes Berkeley's share of the ALPHA antihydrogen program. Jonathan S. Wurtele served as principal investigator. Joel Fajans, the first lead on the grant, died during the award period of 2018 to 2025. ALPHA traps antihydrogen, the antimatter twin of hydrogen. Its spectrum and its fall in gravity can be checked against hydrogen's. Any gap would shake two base rules of physics: CPT symmetry and the weak equivalence principle.

Berkeley's part was plasma craft. The team honed control of the charged clouds used to build and hold antihydrogen. They built field probes that read the trap's magnet grid in place. One find stands out: stray patch fields on trap walls explain lost antiprotons and weak trapping after ionization. The gravity trap work fed the ALPHA-g fall test. Data methods for that test also came from this grant.
doe-osti-3376118-thermal-and-electromech:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229875-2026-TECH, dated June 2026, studies the thin carbon strips that polarimeters shoot through particle beams. F. Rathmann heads a multi-author team. A polarimeter strip must be thin enough to barely disturb the beam, yet it soaks up heat with each bunch pass. In a relativistic bunched beam, that heat lands in sharp pulses. The strip can glow, sag, or creep, and each flaw bends the reading.

The note models the strip as it scans across the beam. Plots track strip heat along its length at set times near the beam-center crossing. Peak marks run near twenty-five hundred kelvin in the shown case. That case uses the Electron-Ion Collider flattop with a cooled emittance beam. The scan speed comes from a project table of reference values. Both the heat path and the strip's pull-and-bend response are in scope.
doe-osti-3376147-queued-up-2026-edition-:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory slide deck Queued Up: 2026 Edition, by Joseph Rand, Anna Cheyette, Chris Talley, and six more authors, takes the yearly census of grid queues. The snapshot is dated June 2026 and covers queues at the end of 2025. Each hopeful plant must ask its grid operator for a link. The line is long, and most in it will never build. The deck turns that raw queue data into charts on what, where, and how much.

The team pulled data from seven grid operators and fifty other balancing areas. Fine print flags gaps: dates are missing for some plants, so some cuts drop them. One trend stands out in bold type. More than 750 gigawatts of queued capacity was withdrawn in 2025 alone. Working and withdrawn volumes both trend up year by year. The deck is the field's standard scorecard for the grid link backlog.
doe-osti-3377661-battery-energy-storage-:
Taylor Curtis of the National Laboratory of the Rockies covers the end of life of large battery energy storage systems in slides dated April 2026. The deck treats both performance decline and decommissioning, the legal step of retiring a site. Large systems using current lithium-ion technology have an expected performance lifetime of 15 to 20 years, depending on duty cycle, operating conditions, and performance thresholds.

Expected lifetimes have risen fast: lithium iron phosphate and nickel manganese cobalt systems were commonly expected to run about 10 years in 2020 and 16 years by 2022. Planned augmentation or repowering can push a project past 20 years. The second half surveys state decommissioning rules, with Texas and Oregon as detailed examples of site restoration duties.
doe-osti-3382439-em-erratum-to-em-the-sc: Los Alamos National Laboratory erratum LA-UR-26-26136, issued July 21, 2026, by Joshua D. Carmichael and Jonas A. Kintner, corrects their article on the scaling and units of the elastic response term for Rayleigh waves output by the Computer Programs in Seismology package. A short correction note, it fixes two notational errors: the fractions inside the definitions of two unitless terms following Equation 9 were inverted. It supplies the secular equation the original omitted, defining the non-dispersive Rayleigh wave speed for waves sampling only the top layer of a geological model.
doe-osti-3383409-impacts-of-dual-use-sol:
The University of Massachusetts Amherst closes award DE-EE0009374 with a final technical report, dated July 24, 2026. The subject is the impacts of dual-use solar, or agrivoltaics, on crop productivity and the agricultural economy in Massachusetts and beyond. Dwayne Breger, director of Clean Energy Extension, is the principal investigator named on the filing. The project period ran from October 1, 2021 to December 31, 2025, under the Solar Energy Technologies Office.

Agrivoltaics puts solar panels and farming on the same land. The land earns twice, but each use constrains the other. The questions are practical. How much do crops yield in the panels' shade and pattern? And what does that mean for farm income and the wider agricultural economy? The 56-page report is the project's final account of what it measured and concluded.
doe-osti-3413710-printability-and-mechan:
Report ORNL/TM-2026/4696 from Oak Ridge National Laboratory, dated July 2026, tests printability and strength of two nickel alloys made by laser powder bed fusion. Sebastien Dryepondt leads a six-author team. The alloys are 625 and 244, both used where heat and corrosion bite hard.

Printed samples showed cell structures with rich carbides along cell walls. After 100 hours at heat, no creep cavities were found in the sample studied. By 360 hours, new precipitates had formed and grown. Tracking such changes tells engineers how printed nickel parts age under load at high heat. Creep samples were imaged again at set times to track precipitate change over time.
doe-osti-3413712-performance-and-reliabi:
In August 2026, Oak Ridge National Laboratory released report ORNL/TM-2026/4684, which walks through the ARM Data Advisor, a helper tool for climate data users. Christian Mark Salvador leads an eight-author team. ARM is the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement program, which runs climate observation sites worldwide. Its data archive is vast and hard to search.

Sample chats show the advisor at work. One user asked about ozone and fine particles at the Bankhead National Forest site for May 2025. The advisor noted which data streams exist there and which do not. It then suggested workable data sets. New users can find climate data without knowing archive codes.
doe-osti-3452323-sparc-the-impact-of-900:
Oak Ridge SPaRC study by Emilio Piesciorovsky, Matthew DeMorat, and Laura Ann Anderson tests how 900 megahertz internet-of-things devices affect transfer trip protection. Crowded radio bands can disturb relay messages that trip breakers. The study mixes lab relays with emulated channels.

Current curves show maximum load currents stay below trip and fuse limits. Fault currents at both line ends are plotted for one relay type. The scheme trips the far breaker to clear line faults quickly. Utilities learn whether cheap wireless sensors can safely share crowded spectrum with protection gear safely.
doe-osti-3818488-scalable-charge-transpo:
A final technical report closes award DE-EE0009524 for Georgia Tech, covering September 2021 to September 2025. Juan-Pablo Correa-Baena is principal investigator, with John Reynolds and Sanggyun Kim among the team. Perovskite solar cells need thin layers that carry charge out of the light-absorbing film. Standard layers fade under heat and long running. The project built new layers meant to scale: polymers for holes, small molecules for electrons.

Cells using the new layers reached efficiencies near eighteen percent, close to the best standard stacks. Their edge was endurance under heat and steady light. Flat, stacking-friendly chains drove the polymer results. Not every target was met: polymer electron layers lagged, and the harshest heat aging goals went unmet, so the team pivoted toward small molecule electron layers. The report ends with design rules and next steps.
doe-osti-3818599-solar-feasibility-study:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5R00-97358, dated September 2026, judges solar options for the Bureau of Reclamation at Glen Canyon, Arizona. Otto Van Geet and James Elsworth are the printed authors. The team scored five spots for panels beside Glen Canyon Dam. They were the warehouse roof, a warehouse carport, and an aggregate supply yard west of the dam. That yard plus park service land formed a fourth option, and the dam's east gate a fifth.

The warehouse roof alone can hold a one hundred kilowatt direct-current array with room to spare. Its switchgear can take the feed, though a crane must lift the gear up. Each site gets layout, wiring, and cost treatment under shared price rules. The study gives the bureau a ranked base for funding talks.
doe-osti-3917644-compact-catalytic-membr:
E2H2NANO, LLC closes out a four-year Energy Department award with this final technical report on a compact reactor that makes ammonia in one step. Shoujie Ren led the project, with the University of South Carolina and the University at Buffalo as partners. The work ran from April 2021 to April 2025 under award DE-EE0009409.

The device joins a catalyst with a membrane, so ammonia forms and is pulled out in the same unit, at milder heat and pressure than standard plants need. Tests tracked how the membrane moves ammonia gas at varied feed strengths and pressures, and how those choices change flow rates. Smaller, gentler ammonia plants could cut the energy bill of a chemical now made in huge, hot factories. The report gives the design and test record behind that claim.
dr-johnson-s-works-life-poems-and-tales-:
Volume one of the nine-volume Works of Samuel Johnson, printed in 1825, gathers the life, poems, and tales of the great English writer. An opening advertisement claims that no British author, not even Addison, offers a richer store of sound instruction and rational entertainment. The editors promise a correct text with notes that now and then censure Johnson's own faults.

Poems fill much of the hosted text. Odes to Stella and evening pieces sit beside verses printed among Mrs. Williams's Miscellanies, with lines urging a regulated heart that stays consistent through change. Letters and small lives, among them George Psalmanazar and Mr. Bower, show Johnson as a biographer of odd and fallen men. The volume gives readers the young and middle Johnson whole: poet, essayist, and maker of English prose style.
fardorougha-the-miser-the-works-of-willi:
Carleton's Fardorougha, The Miser opens the first volume of his collected works. William Carleton wrote the Irish tale in eight parts. Part I begins on a clear August night with moon and stars. A horseman rides up a narrow lane to a whitewashed cottage.

He knocks hard and asks if Mary Moan is at home. A broad face in flannel nightcap folds answers from a small window. The messenger bears news about Honor Donovan, Fardorougha's wife of thirteen years. Something long awaited has at last come, he hints. The village voice of the telling is broad and comic. Carleton renders Irish speech with loving exactness. The miser's household stands at the tale's center.
france-and-england-in-north-america-part:
Parkman tells how the valleys of the Mississippi and the Lakes were revealed to the world. The chief actor in those daring enterprises wrote much but printed nothing, he warns. Most of this volume's new material comes from the public archives of France.

The sampled scene belongs to La Salle's Illinois country. Iroquois warriors, having burned a town, grow uneasy as the Illinois appear on the low hills. They ask Tonty to act as mediator, and he crosses the meadow gladly. Francis Parkman published this third part of his series, The Discovery of the Great West, in 1870.
glinda-of-oz-in-which-are-related-the-ex:
L Frank Baum closed his own Oz series with Glinda of Oz, dedicated to his son Robert Stanton Baum. Princess Ozma and Dorothy travel to stop a war between the Flatheads and the Skeezers, crossing mist maidens and a magic stairway to a flat-topped mountain. Queen Coo-ee-oh rules the Skeezers' magic isle under a glass dome.

The visitors are trapped when the isle submerges, fishes pressing against the transparent dome, and Glinda the Good must mount a rescue with all Oz's counselors. Baum raises real stakes: queens drown, tyrants scheme, and Ozma's peaceful authority is tested. Published after his death, the book is darker and more elaborate than earlier Oz tales, and many readers rank it among the finest.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BrownleeWanda_B: On October 29, 1979, a letter went to Dr. Mary S. Metz of Hood College concerning Wanda Brownlee. The letter is attributed, probably, to Harold Weisberg, whose files hold it and whose correspondence ranged across everyone the assassination case touched, academics included. What Weisberg wanted from a Hood College professor about Brownlee sits inside the letter itself. The letter is kept as part of the Weisberg correspondence preserved in the archive.
journal-of-researches-into-the-natural-h:
Charles Darwin's Journal of Researches records his voyage round the world in H.M.S. Beagle. Darwin sailed as naturalist under Captain Fitz Roy. This edition, reprinted in 1913, covers the natural history and geology of every country visited. Darwin dedicates it to Charles Lyell, the geologist whose work shaped his own.

Darwin says plainly that whatever merit his books hold came largely from studying Lyell's writings. The journal itself made his name before the Origin of Species appeared. In it, a young observer describes fossils, islands, volcanoes, and strange living species. His exact, eager notes let readers watch a great scientist forming his questions. The Beagle journal remains a classic of travel and science together.
judith-a-play-in-three-acts-founded-on-t:
Arnold Bennett wrote this play in three acts, first published in London in 1919 and first staged that April at the Devonshire Park Theatre in Eastbourne. Bennett took his plot from the apocryphal Book of Judith. His heroine is the widow Judith of Bethulia, a Hebrew city besieged by the Assyrian army of the general Holofernes, and Lillah McCarthy played the part at the first performance.

The action moves from a street in Bethulia to the valley by the Assyrian camp and into Holofernes' tent, then back to the city on the next day. Elders Ozias, Chabris, and Charmis speak for the trapped city, while Bagoas and Achior serve the Assyrian side. Readers get a tight stage version of the old story, built on talk, dread, and one woman's resolve.
minstrelsy-of-the-scottish-border-volume:
Volume Two of Walter Scott's Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border continues his ballad collection. This third edition is dated 1806. The historical ballads here include Lesley's March and the Battle of Philiphaugh. Others recall the battles of Pentland Hills, Loudonhill, and Bothwell Bridge.

A second part turns from history to romantic ballads. It opens with an ode on Scottish music and an introduction to the Tale of Tamlane. The Young Tamlane and Erlinton follow. Scott prints each ballad with learned notes, preserving songs of covenanting wars and fairy legend side by side. The notes explain each ballad's history and sources.
modern-eloquence-vol-ii-after-dinner-spe:
Thomas B. Reed edited this second volume of Modern Eloquence, a library of speeches and addresses. His associate editors were Justin McCarthy, Rossiter Johnson, and Albert Ellery Bergh. The volume collects after-dinner speeches by speakers whose names run from E to O. A color frontispiece reproduces George W. Maynard's mural Justice from the Library of Congress.

The mural shows Justice holding a globe and an upright naked sword. It belongs to a series of eight panels of the virtues. After-dinner speaking was a serious art in Reed's America, and anthologies like this preserved its models. Reed, a former Speaker of the House, knew oratory from the inside.
mormon-settlement-in-arizona-a-record-of:
James H. McClintock, Arizona's historian, published this record in 1921. His subtitle calls it a record of peaceful conquest of the desert. Chapter One treats Mormon colonization across the West. McClintock credits the pioneers as first farmers in many states, who kept the wilderness broken.

Chapter Two follows the Mormon Battalion of the Mexican War. The battalion marched through the Southwest, took the pueblo of Tucson, and mapped the way through Arizona. Cooke's and Tyler's records, plus soldiers' journals, supply the detail. Chapter Three covers the muster-out and the battalion men who became Arizonans. The book documents irrigation colonies that made desert farming possible.
nasa-tm-19650012562-lunar-landing-dynami:
J Bensko and J L Cortez, in the Physics and Astrophysics Branch at Marshall, wrote this progress report in October 1962. It supports a study of a lunar logistics vehicle, a craft meant to carry supplies to the Moon. Their topic was how much lunar surface models varied, and what that meant for landing.

Nobody yet knew the Moon's surface well. Models of its strength and texture differed widely. Landing gear designed for the wrong surface could fail. Bensko and Cortez set out the range of models then in use. That range told designers how much uncertainty their landing dynamics had to cover.
nasa-tm-19650019799-rotor-stator-interac:
William L Copeland and John L Crigler at Langley presented this noise study in Austin, Texas, in October 1964. Inside an axial-flow compressor, spinning rotor blades pass fixed stator blades. Their interaction makes noise. The team used a single-stage research compressor to study that noise where it spreads into the far field.

Results are given as radiation patterns and frequency spectra. The measured patterns matched calculated results fairly well, the authors report. Compressor noise matters for aircraft that use such machinery. Understanding where the sound goes, and at what pitches, is a first step toward quieter designs for later engines.
nasa-tm-19660024034-supersonic-aerodynam:
Kyle E Wiggins and George E Kaattari present results for a family of triangular wing models at supersonic speeds. Leading edges were swept sixty degrees in the sample's wording, and attack angles ran from slightly negative up to ninety degrees. Speeds covered three settings in the Mach three to Mach five range. The team reports lift, drag, and pitching moment for the family, plus lift-to-drag ratios.

Apex bluntness and cross-section shape were varied to see their effects. A slab model with tip controls and trailing edge flaps also appears. Triangular, or delta, planforms served fighters and entry vehicles alike. Broad test sweeps like this one gave designers a map of the whole family, not just one favored shape.
nasa-tm-19670005590-exposition-of-sundma:
Donald K. Yeomans, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this exposition in December 1966. It explains Sundman's regularization of the three-body problem, the classic puzzle of predicting how three bodies move under their shared gravity. Ordinary equations break down when two bodies collide, and regularization rewrites them so the math stays usable.

Yeomans derives the equations of motion and the integrals of motion in full. He examines a double collision, where two bodies meet while the third stays apart. A new variable removes the singularity at collision, and the distances are expanded as power series in that variable. A second variable removes singularities for any number of such collisions. The series solutions work, he finds, but they converge extremely slowly.
nasa-tm-19680007011-supersonic-aerodynam:
Clyde Hayes, at the Langley Research Center in Virginia, wrote this memorandum in February 1968. Numbered TM X-1491, it reports the supersonic aerodynamic characteristics of a model of an air-to-ground missile. The missile used folding control wings near its midbody, so the model represented both boost and glide configurations.

Wind-tunnel runs at Mach 1.60 and 2.00 varied fin size and sweep angle, plus control wing size and deflection, at two roll angles. The body-fin combination proved generally stable across the tested fin sizes and sweeps. One exception appeared at the higher Mach number and steepest fin sweep, where instability showed at larger angles of attack. Adding the control wings barely changed longitudinal stability but raised normal force and axial force substantially. Deflecting the wings produced useful side and normal forces with almost no pitching or yawing disturbance. The wing fold slots had no aerodynamic effect.
nasa-tm-19680015291-feasibility-of-deter:
C. Prabhakara wrote this May 1968 Goddard Space Flight Center report, numbered X-622-68-203, while linked to the Goddard Institute for Space Studies. He asks whether satellites can measure ozone, the gas high in the air that blocks harmful sunlight, by watching infrared energy leaving Earth. Sharp readings near one ozone band are the key evidence in his test.

Prabhakara builds a method from heat transfer theory and a simple two-part model of how ozone spreads with height. He then checks the method on four case studies and studies its errors with care. His warning is plain: a small error in the measured light grows much larger in the ozone value drawn from it.
nasa-tm-19690003887-hypersonic-aerodynam:
Bernard Spencer Jr. of Langley Research Center tested a logistics spacecraft model at hypersonic speed in this report. The low-fineness-ratio concept used variable geometry for its mission. A fold-down wing stayed stowed during entry, then deployed at subsonic speeds for better low-speed performance.

Tests ran in the Langley 15-inch hypersonic apparatus at Mach 10.03, with the wing retracted. Adding outboard tails raised maximum lift-drag ratio and gave stability across the test range. Two tail sweep options were compared. Varying tail dihedral produced a useful range of trim angles of attack. Elevon deflections widened the trimmable range further. Positive effective dihedral held for all configurations tested, with some reduction at high tail dihedral.
nasa-tm-19700026474-some-effects-of-rada:
Thomas E. Moore prepared this Apollo internal note, number 67-MI-20, for the Manned Spacecraft Center. It studies how the position of the radar antenna affects the lunar module's descent. Radar gives the guidance computer fresh height readings on the way down, and where its antenna sits decides when those readings can begin.

A hybrid simulation compared descent performance for three radar start heights over a realistic lunar terrain model. The study scores each case on fuel-related velocity cost, pitch swings before high gate, and viewing time after it. One clear result: the radar should keep updating altitude steadily from well before high gate. Critical beam angles and zero Doppler conditions are tied back to the simulation outcomes.
nasa-tm-19710008423-design-performance-a:
Henry B. Block, Lawrence A. Mueller, and Fred Boecker Jr. of the Lewis Research Center report here on four large electric heat sources. The heaters were built for liquid-metal systems tied to the SNAP-8 power program. On the ground, they stood in for a nuclear reactor's heat.

Two heaters were compact units that copied the reactor's heat behavior closely. The other two were heavy-duty units built above all for reliability. The first pair was built at one power level, and the second pair at a higher one. The paper covers their design, their performance, and what test runs taught the team.
nasa-tm-19710016878-hypersonic-aerodynam:
Charles L Ladson of the Langley Research Center wrote this April 1970 memorandum, NASA TM X-1994. It reports force tests on the DL-4, a lifting entry vehicle shape. Such winged shapes glide back through the atmosphere instead of falling like a capsule. The test shape had a lift to drag ratio near three, strong for a reentry craft.

Ladson gathered data at Mach 6 and Mach 10 in air, and Mach 20 in helium. He compared the readings with theory to find where the math held and where it failed. Separate Mach 10 runs tried tip fin and body changes. The goal was a shape stable around all three axes during entry.
nasa-tm-19710018639-effects-of-retrorock:
Edwin E Davenport and Edwin E Lee Jr of the Langley Research Center studied how retrorocket exhaust changes the drag of a blunt cone. The shape was a one hundred twenty degree cone, like the aeroshell of a planetary entry craft. Braking rockets firing forward into the airflow could disturb that flow. The team tested the idea in the Langley sixteen foot transonic tunnel.

Blunted cones carried simulated retrothrust nozzles with four, eight, or twelve jets. Runs held the cone at zero angle of attack and low subsonic speeds. The results showed a strong interaction between the exhaust and the drag. Once heat shield needs were met, dropping the front cone face would help.
observations-on-the-effects-of-the-corn-:
Thomas Robert Malthus wrote this short work on trade in grain. It was printed in London in 1814. Malthus taught political economy at the East India College. He wrote as Parliament prepared to review the Corn Laws. Those laws controlled imports of grain into Britain.

Malthus asks how the laws affect farming and national wealth. He also asks what happens when corn prices rise or fall. He argues that earlier debate missed key points on both sides. He answers Adam Smith on the bounty for exporting corn. The work offers a clear case in an old policy fight. He writes in a calm, reasoned style for lawmakers.
ohio-biological-survey-bull-10-vol-11-no:
Bruce Fink wrote part four of The Ascomycetes of Ohio. Leafy Corrington wrote part five in the same bulletin. Ohio State University published the bulletin in 1921. Part four treats the lichen family called Lecideaceae. Part five treats the family called Peltigeraceae.

Fink explains how lichens fit among other ascomycete fungi. He notes close links to related lichen families. He uses the language of modern systematic mycology. The papers classify species and describe their structures. They served working botanists who identify Ohio lichens in the field. Careful keys and notes support that field work throughout.
on-the-art-of-writing-lectures-delivered:
Arthur Quiller-Couch delivered these lectures at Cambridge in 1913 and 1914. Cambridge University Press first published them in 1916. Quiller-Couch held the King Edward chair of English there. He was also a fellow of Jesus College. The book opens with his inaugural lecture.

The lectures teach students how to write clear English. Quiller-Couch stresses plain words, order, and honest thought. He warns against jargon and empty, showy phrases. His spoken style keeps the lectures lively and direct. Generations of students learned style from this book. It remains a classic manual for young writers.
podcast-joerogan-WDqWc_ucs-o:
Neuroscientist Amishi Jha joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1723 to talk about attention. Jha studies how the mind focuses and wanders, and she has tested mindfulness training on soldiers, students, and surgeons. Her subject is the one resource every listener feels slipping.

She explains her finding that attention works like a flashlight, strong but easy to knock off target, and that short daily practice can steady it. Rogan asks how phones and stress wear the beam down. The episode turns lab science into a usable skill, with a researcher who speaks in clear, kind terms.
robinson-fewer-and-better-babies-birth-c: A library stamp from the School of Theology at Claremont heads the title page of William J. Robinson's book on birth control. Its headings read Fewer and Better Babies, Birth Control, and By Prevenception. Robinson, M.D., is named as chief of a Bronx hospital department and editor of The Critic and Guide. A long list of his earlier books fills the page, on sexual disorders, married life, eugenics, and sex knowledge. An introduction by another hand is promised at the page's foot. No contents or chapter is shown.
the-american-nation-a-history-volume-1-e: Only a Project Gutenberg header is present here, with no book pages at all. The header names the work as European Background of American History, by Edward Potts Cheyney, and calls it volume one of The American Nation: A History. It gives the file as etext number 4089, in English, at edition 10, first posted November 21, 2001, with a May 2003 release date. Nothing of Cheyney's own text follows the header.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-05-mar:
March 1858 brings The Atlantic Monthly's readers to the catacombs of Rome. A line from Dante's Paradiso heads the piece, and the writer calls the ground below the city Roma Sotterranea, an underground Rome of the dead. Sacred, he says, is the dust of its narrow streets, and blessed were those laid there for their faith.

The words in pace, in peace, mark the graves in that buried city. The upper city holds great memories, the essay grants, but none greater than these below. Christian Rome's heroes, it argues, matched republican Rome's in courage and devotion, while a new spirit shone from their deeds over the world.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-06-apr:
April 1858 opens with personal memories of the Hundred Days, the span from March 20 to June 28, 1815, when Napoleon came back from Elba and Louis the Eighteenth lost his throne. The writer calls the span as gripping as it was eventful, and notes that curiosity about it has not yet tired.

Anyone who can add a personal touch to that epoch, he says, should set it down in familiar form, to give the tale the strongest stamp of truth. He himself was then a schoolboy in Paris, at a school tied to one of the national lyceums. His small witness joins the grand story of a star of destiny rising once more before it sank forever.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-03-no-17-mar:
Holbein and the Dance of Death leads the March 1859 Atlantic, starting not with the artist but with the town of Bâle. It stands at the northwest corner of Switzerland, where the Rhine turns from running west between Germany and Switzerland to running north between Germany and France.

That perch on three borders gives the town and its people a mixed air. They are like a stranger in a new colony. He wears too much of his old dress to pass for a native. He wears too little to be taken for a foreigner. Rome was already old, the essay notes, when the Emperor Valentinian built a fortress there called Basilia, and houses soon gathered around it.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-03-no-18-apr:
Agrarianism, the April 1859 lead essay, frames society's oldest quarrel as a war between two houses: the House of Have and the House of Want. The strife is older than the fable of the bramble crowned king of the trees, its cited authority holds, and it still rages in the writer's own century.

Herodotus knew it, and so must every later historian. No race stands outside it, from Tartars cooking meat beneath their saddles to Sybarites put out by a wrinkled rose leaf. The essay marches the feud through Spartans and Athenians, Roman orders high and low, Norman lords and Saxon serfs, down to slaveholders in Carolina and farmers in New England.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-05-no-29-mar:
The French Character leads the March 1860 Atlantic. The American character, it begins, is now widely granted to be the most open to the world of modern times. An American, all else equal, is likelier than others to judge foreign peoples without fixed rules of thumb.

Before travel between Europe and the United States grew common, Americans took their notions of the French, and of Italian skies, from English books. Their first picture of the Gallic race ran largely to the absurd: wild tales of sickly self-love, stingy fine eating, strained manners, and light folly, each with a Frenchman for its hero. First meetings in person often seemed to confirm the prejudice, the essay grants.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-05-no-30-apr:
April 1860 leads with The Laws of Beauty. Many hunters after the line of beauty, it argues, have made one fatal mistake: they sought in what is outward for what lies within. Beauty, known by the mind alone, must express intelligence.

It cannot spring from chance or from mere matter, but from forces of the spirit. A figure's outline can speak the mind's feelings. Sculpture proves it, showing living faces in cold marble. Engraving proves it too. Its simple lines can soothe with a lowland scene or brace with mountain air. The highest beauty, the essay holds, is that which expresses the noblest feeling, like the shining face of Moses.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-07-no-41-mar:
German Universities: The Professors leads the March 1861 Atlantic. Which German school best fits his purpose, the essay asks, is the question of many an American student who has finished his course at home and looks abroad to complete his studies.

Of Göttingen and Heidelberg he will have read and heard much, and Berlin's newer fame will not be strange to him. But Tübingen, Würzburg, Erlangen, Halle, or even Bonn may be little more than names, since few of his countrymen study there. Most have followed the stream of the last century to Göttingen or Heidelberg, perhaps with a winter in Berlin, and found them good. The essay asks whether Munich, Leipzig, or Jena might serve many a student better.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-07-no-42-apr:
April Days, headed by a line from In Memoriam asking whether trouble can dwell with April days, leads the April 1861 Atlantic. In methodical New England life, the essay says, some magic is still granted to summer. Most people resign themselves to being decently happy in June, at least.

They praise June's weather, having spent the cold earlier months in the city, and they will flee the hot later ones for a barren seacoast. God offers a necklace of twelve pearls each year, and most men pick the fairest, label it June, and throw the rest away. The essay sings instead for the days of late April, when an Italian warmth broods over the hills in a glistening mist.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-09-no-53-mar:
March 1862 leads with the fruits of free labor in the smaller islands of the British West Indies. Freeing an enslaved race seems, at first thought, a most unsure and perilous undertaking, the essay grants. Everything must be reversed at once.

In place of habits of idleness bred by force must come the pleasure of activity or the pull of distant good. Forethought, alertness, and craft must be planted where labor was stolid and unthinking. A people timid and dependent must gain self-reliance and courage for unknown tasks, and self-control must replace rule by masters. In a word, a free man must be made out of a born slave, which looks like the hardest task a lawmaker could face.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-09-no-54-apr:
A Letter to a Young Contributor leads the April 1862 Atlantic. My dear young gentleman or young lady, it begins, noting that many a Cecil Dreeme of letters signs a bold man's name in a woman's fine hand. The writer gathers many urgent private letters into one printed reply.

So large a share of Atlantic readers might, would, could, or should write for it too, he says, that the letter is sure of readers, though Mrs. Stowe go uncut and the Autocrat rest an hour. He does not dream that writers will stop judging a magazine by its handling of their own last piece. A young lady, he jokes, judges a ball by her own luck in partners in just the same way.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-11-no-65-mar:
Christopher North leads the March 1863 Atlantic, and the essay starts with Plutarch's own rule for life-writing. Setting out on the crowded lives of Alexander and Caesar, Plutarch warned that his design was not histories but lives.

The most glorious feats, Plutarch held, do not always give the clearest signs of a man's virtue or vice. A small matter, a saying or a jest, often tells more of character than famous sieges or the bloodiest battles. As portrait painters take most care with the face, where character is seen, so the life-writer may dwell on marks of the soul and leave great battles to others. The essay sets those rules up as sound before turning to its subject.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-11-no-66-apr:
April 1863 leads with Joseph Severn's paper on the ups and downs of Keats's fame. An editor's note says Severn scarcely needs presenting to Atlantic readers. It reprints Shelley's tribute from the preface to Adonais, written in 1821.

Keats, Shelley wrote, was accompanied to Rome and tended in his last illness by Severn, a young artist of the highest promise. Severn almost risked his own life and gave up every prospect for unwearied care of his dying friend. Had Shelley known it in time, he would have added his full praise to the firmer reward a good man finds in recalling his own motives. Severn's conduct, Shelley said, boded well for his career.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-13-no-77-mar:
The Queen of California leads the March 1864 Atlantic. The writer can see the excitement this title wakes as it flashes across the sierras, down the valleys, and into the reading-rooms and parlors of the Golden City of the Golden State.

When the San Francisco Bulletin announces the piece, he imagines, every favored circle will contest who the queen may be. Is it the blond maiden who led a string of hearts in a leash when she left? The essay plays with that guessing game before naming its own sovereign of California life, keeping the reader in suspense through its opening pages.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-13-no-78-apr:
Fighting Facts for Fogies leads the April 1864 Atlantic with a defence of the young. They stand accused, it says, of slighting the past. The writer pleads them guilty and glad of it: a past that showed them no care has earned no care back.

He goes further. On the old methods of rearing children, he argues, the race ought long ago to have died out. There was too little that was humane in the process. Fathers and mothers of the sternest old type treated birth almost as a deed of ownership. A helpless newcomer, on their view, could be held in lasting chains as a kind of slave.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-20-no-117-ju: Volume twenty of The Atlantic Monthly, printed at Boston by Ticknor and Fields in 1867, is present only as a volume title page and the start of an alphabetical contents list. Early entries name An Artist's Dream by T. W. Higginson on page 100, The Autobiography of a Quack in two parts, A Native of Bornoo, and The Bowery at Night by Charles Dawson Shanly on page 602. No article text appears in these pages.
the-destiny-of-the-soul-a-critical-histo: William Rounseville Alger's The Destiny of the Soul, a critical history of the doctrine of a future life. It appears in a tenth edition from Roberts Brothers of Boston, dated 1880, with six new chapters. The title page promises a bibliography by Ezra Abbot of the Harvard Divinity School. It covers 4,977 books on the nature, origin, and destiny of the soul, classified by date, with notes and indexes. A note says the bibliography is not included here. Only the title pages and the preface's opening line are present here.
the-life-and-most-surprising-adventures-: Daniel Defoe tale of Robinson Crusoe first appeared in 1719, and this record follows an 1801 edition that gathers many versions into one. Only the editorial notes and the start of the title page are present here. Those notes explain how later editions folded in further adventures and an angelic vision tale. Even an account of Alexander Selkirk marooning joined some editions. The Crusoe narrative itself is absent from this record beyond that explanation.
the-life-of-col-james-gardiner-who-was-s: P. Doddridge wrote the life of Colonel James Gardiner, who was slain at the battle of Prestonpans on September 21, 1745. Only the title page and a chapter list are present here, tracing Gardiner parentage, the battle of Ramillies, military promotion, checks of conscience, and a conversion. Later chapters promise letters, devotion and charity, and death apprehensions before Prestonpans. Two appendices and a note on his personal appearance close the plan. The biography itself is absent from this record.
the-life-of-columbus-from-his-own-letter:
Edward Everett Hale built his life of Columbus from the admiral own letters, journals, and other papers of his time. A preface links the book to the four hundredth anniversary of 1492. Hale praises Washington Irving great Columbus biography as a noble model of diligent work.

Hale then parts from Irving plan. Irving folded in the whole West India history and much Spanish court history, while Hale follows Columbus personal fortunes closely. Background gets only the space needed to explain those fortunes. Contemporary papers guide the account wherever Hale could find them.
the-marvelous-exploits-of-paul-bunyan-as:
W. B. Laughead wrote and illustrated The Marvelous Exploits of Paul Bunyan, published by the Red River Lumber Company for the amusement of its friends. The tales were collected from the camps of white pine lumbermen, who had carried them through the North Woods from Maine to California over generations. A historical note traces the company from log drives down the Red River of the North to its Minnesota mills.

An editorial note explains that the stories first appeared in small company booklets in 1914 and 1916, then in a 1922 book on Paul Bunyan and his big blue ox. Later printings followed in 1924, 1927, 1931, and 1934. Laughead admits that the names of supporting characters, including the animals, are his own inventions. Readers get the giant lumberjack's feats in the form that first carried camp folklore into print.
the-people-s-common-sense-medical-advise: R. V. Pierce, M.D., wrote The People's Common Sense Medical Adviser in Plain English, or Medicine Simplified. The title page calls Pierce a consulting physician at the Invalids' Hotel and Surgical Institute and president of the World's Dispensary Medical Association. This is the fifty-fourth edition, entered in 1895. Only the title page and dedication are present here, so the medical advice itself does not appear. Pierce dedicates the work to his patients across America and abroad.
the-pony-rider-boys-with-the-texas-range:
Frank Gee Patchin's The Pony Rider Boys with the Texas Rangers, or On the Trail of the Border Bandits, lists twenty-four chapters of mounting trouble. Titles promise excitement on the West Fork and a mysterious attack. They promise a much-wanted desperado, the boys initiated, and fun on mountain trails. Fancy shots, a cave of the bandits, and a perilous position come before the conclusion.

Chapter I leaves the main branch of Delaware Creek, broad and slow, on its way to the muddy Pecos River. It turns up the west branch. Horses and men are wearied, dusty, and sleepy under a midsummer Texas sun. Little has been said for some time. The riders work south by west toward a line of green foliage. For five hours it has looked a short distance away, and it seems no nearer than when they first sighted it in the morning.
the-religions-of-japan-from-the-dawn-of-: William Elliot Griffis, formerly of the Imperial University of Tokio, published his history with Scribner's at New York in 1895, spanning Japanese religion from earliest times to the Meiji era. A long dedication honors the faculty of Union Theological Seminary and three English students, Ernest Satow, William Aston, and Basil Chamberlain, as founders of critical scholarship on Japan. Here only the title pages and dedication are present, so the history itself does not appear.
theory-of-the-earth-with-proofs-and-illu: James Hutton, M.D. and fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, published his Theory of the Earth in 1795. Volume one presents part one, examining how strata are composed, dissolved, and restored. Sections treat the operations that consolidate strata and raise land above the sea. Later chapters answer Kirwan's objections to an igneous origin for stony substances, and refute the idea of primitive mountains. A contents listing is what is included in this record, so Hutton's arguments themselves do not appear.

Volume two of James Hutton's Theory of the Earth, published in 1795, carries part two of his four-part work. Its contents promise further facts and observations supporting the geological theory. Chapters gather evidence for land being elevated above the surface of the sea. Examples come from different countries, and later chapters treat the surface dissolving again and soil forming for plants. Hutton's system depends on slow cycles of decay and renewal. Only the contents pages are on these pages, so his evidence itself is not shown.
throwing-sticks-in-the-national-museum-t:
Otis T. Mason, curator of ethnology, described throwing-sticks held by the United States National Museum in a paper reprinted from the Smithsonian report for 1883 to 1884. The Government Printing Office issued it at Washington in 1890, with plates one to seventeen. Throwing-sticks extend and hook a thrown weapon.

Mason cites Col. Lane Fox's three regions: Australia, the Upper Amazon among the Conibos and Purus peoples, and Arctic North America. The museum holds few Australian examples and none from Amazonia, so his paper concentrates on northern specimens. Readers get early museum ethnology about hunting tools across continents.
washington-and-his-comrades-in-arms-a-ch:
George M. Wrong, a Canadian historian, wrote Washington and His Comrades in Arms as volume twelve of the Chronicles of America series, issued by Yale University Press in 1921. His prefatory note, signed at the University of Toronto on June 15, 1920, admits a certain audacity. He is a Briton writing on Washington for a company of American writers, and he doubted his own fitness for the task.

The editor and publishers, he says, pressed the work on him, holding that Americans would not find a British reading of Washington unwelcome just then. He thanks the editor for wise criticism. He thanks Worthington Chauncey Ford, a great Washington authority of the Massachusetts Historical Society, for reading the proofs. The book then tells the war of independence through Washington and the men who fought beside him, with a neighbor's sympathy and a scholar's care.
wee-peter-pug-the-story-of-a-bit-of-misc: Ernest Aris wrote and pictured Wee Peter Pug, the story of a bit of mischief and what came of it, for the Saalfield Publishing Company of Chicago, Akron, and New York. Pages present here hold the picture book's title pages and its first line only, so the mischief itself is not shown. The story opens in rhyme, with a dame who has lost her shoe. Peter Pug is a small dog hero for the youngest readers, drawn in Saalfield's bold style for cheap color books.
world-s-war-events-v-volume-3-beginning-: Francis J. Reynolds and Allen L. Churchill compiled this third volume of World's War Events, published in 1919. Pages present here hold title pages and a frontispiece showing Allied commanders, but no narrative text. The volume's stated span runs from the first American destroyers sailing abroad in April 1917 to the peace treaties.
